visits.text: Calcutta (Kolkata): eventful arrival after an interrupted journey, major colonial city of the British empire in India.
Administrative districts and Hooghly quays: formalities, embarkation and organization of the rest of the journey to Hong Kong.

Train from Gaya (closest station to Bodhgaya) to Kolkata (about 7 hours—take the Rajdhani or Duronto Express). Kolkata, formerly Calcutta, was the British Raj capital until 1911. It's a city of violent contrasts: colonial splendor and misery, vibrant intellectual culture and urban chaos. Start with Victoria Memorial, a white marble palace built between 1906 and 1921 honoring Queen Victoria. Its architecture blends Italian Renaissance, Mughal, and Venetian styles. The museum inside traces Calcutta's history under the British—paintings, weapons, manuscripts, and a reconstruction of the “Black Hole of Calcutta.”

Walk to Howrah Bridge (Rabindra Setu), the world's busiest steel bridge - about 100,000 vehicles and countless pedestrians cross it daily. Built in 1943 without any bolts or rivets (entirely riveted), it spans the Hooghly over 705 meters. The best time to cross on foot is early morning, when flower merchants carry their marigold garlands to Mallick Ghat market just below.

Visit the Indian Museum, India's oldest and largest museum, founded in 1814. Its collections are sprawling: dinosaur fossils, Gandhara Buddhist sculptures, Mughal miniatures, Egyptian mummies, meteorites, and an entire gallery dedicated to Indian textiles. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes—the building is immense.

Tour St Paul's Cathedral, eastern India's largest Gothic building, built in 1847. The stained glass and wooden framework recall English churches, but the tropical climate imposed modifications - airy verandas and large windows. The contrast with Hindu temples is striking.

Your second day in Kolkata focuses on the authentic city. Start at the Mallick Ghat flower market, beneath Howrah Bridge—arrive before 7 am to see mountains of orange marigolds, roses and jasmine unloaded from boats. The colors and energy are incredible. The market has more than 2,000 vendors.

Push on to Kumartuli, the potters' quarter where Durga statues are made for the annual Durga Puja festival—Kolkata's biggest celebration. Hundreds of workshops open to the street mold straw and clay statues reaching up to 5 meters tall. Even outside festival season, watching artisans at work is worth the trip.

Visit Kalighat Temple, one of Hinduism's 51 Shakti Peethas, dedicated to goddess Kali - indeed, Kali gave Calcutta its name. The current temple dates from 1809, but the site has been venerated for centuries. The atmosphere is intense: lines of devotees, flower and incense offerings, priests in trance. Non-Hindus are generally accepted in the outer courtyard.

Head to College Street, the world's largest concentration of bookstores after Buenos Aires. Sidewalks disappear under piles of books - university textbooks, Bengali novels, Tagore poetry, and all sorts of rarities. Coffee House café, an institution since 1942, was Bengali intellectuals' meeting place - Satyajit Ray, Amartya Sen, and Subhas Chandra Bose all hung out here.

activities.text: In the evening, dine at one of the restaurants on Park Street, Kolkata's main dining thoroughfare. Bengali cuisine is considered one of India's most refined—fish (hilsa is king), mustard, five-spice blend (panch phoron), and rasgulla (fresh cheese balls in syrup) for dessert. Kolkata is also the home of puchka (Bengali panipuri)—street vendors serve them everywhere.
Ride a Kolkata tram—it's India's last operating tram network, in service since 1902. The rattling cars cross congested streets at a snail's pace—it's not efficient transport, it's an experience.

Visit Mother Teresa's House (Missionaries of Charity), where the saint lived and worked from 1953 until her death in 1997. Her tomb lies in the ground floor chapel. A small museum traces her life and work among Kolkata's poorest. Entry is free and the place is imbued with moving simplicity.

Take a boat ride on the Hooghly (a branch of the Ganges) at sunset. From the water, you'll see the illuminated Howrah Bridge, Kolkata's ghats, and the old colonial mansions lining the river pass by. Several operators offer one-hour cruises from the Prinsep ghats.

End the evening with a Bengali classical dance or music performance—Kolkata is India's cultural capital, birthplace of Satyajit Ray's cinema and Ravi Shankar's music. The Nandan and Rabindra Sadan venues regularly host events.

places.name: Mumbai

visits.text: Bombay (Mumbai): Fogg and Passepartout's first major immersion in the Indian subcontinent, between colonial station, crowded streets and bustling docks.
Chhatrapati Shivaji Station (inspired by the great colonial stations): departure inland by train toward Calcutta.

You land in Mumbai, and the sensory assault begins the moment you step out of the airport: humid heat, honking horns, the scent of jasmine mingling with exhaust fumes. Grab a taxi or Uber to Colaba or Fort, the historic heart of South Mumbai. Settle in and brace yourself—this city of 20 million doesn't do anything by halves.

Start at the Gateway of India, the monumental yellow basalt arch, 26 meters tall, overlooking the waterfront. Completed in 1924 by Scottish architect George Wittet, it was built to commemorate King George V's 1911 visit—except the king only saw a cardboard model, as construction hadn't yet begun. History's irony: the last official act of the British Empire in India played out here on February 28, 1948, when the 1st Battalion of the Somerset Light Infantry marched through this arch for the final time, with a 21-gun salute. Directly opposite stands the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, opened on December 16, 1903, by industrialist Jamsetji Tata—India's first luxury hotel, which predated the Gateway by 20 years.

Walk north to Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus (CST), formerly Victoria Terminus—the most spectacular train station you'll ever see. A UNESCO site, it was designed by architect Frederick William Stevens in Victorian neo-Gothic style blended with Indian and Islamic elements, completed in 1888 after ten years of construction. Over 3 million passengers pass through daily—making it one of the world's busiest rail hubs. Look up: turrets, stained glass, gargoyles, an octagonal dome crowned by an allegorical statue of Progress holding a torch. You might recognize it—this is where Slumdog Millionaire ends.

A stone's throw from CST, push on to Crawford Market (officially Mahatma Jyotiba Phule Mandai), a Victorian market completed in 1869. The white marble bas-reliefs at the entrance, depicting scenes of rural Indian life, are the work of John Lockwood Kipling—father of Rudyard Kipling, author of The Jungle Book. Inside, it's an assault of colors and smells: pyramids of Alphonso mangoes in season, mountains of turmeric, Kashmiri saffron, loose spices. Arrive before 10 AM for the raw energy of the market in full swing.

Catch the first ferry from the Gateway of India to Elephanta Caves (about 1 hour crossing). The island houses rock-cut temples carved into basalt between the 5th and 7th centuries, UNESCO-listed since 1987. The centerpiece is the Trimurti Sadashiva—a three-faced Shiva over 6 meters tall, representing the Creator, Protector, and Destroyer. It's one of India's largest rock-cut sculptures, and the finesse of the expressions—serenity in the central face, feminine gentleness on the right, ferocity of Bhairava on the left—stops you in your tracks. The Portuguese, who used the sculptures for target practice in the 17th century, caused considerable damage, but what remains is magnificent. NOTE: Closed Mondays. Allow 3 to 4 hours for the complete visit.

Back in Mumbai, stop at Dhobi Ghat, the world's largest open-air laundry, in operation for over 120 years. From the pedestrian bridge at Mahalaxmi station, you'll see hundreds of washermen beating clothes in concrete troughs stretching as far as the eye can see—a hypnotic spectacle and a stark reminder that in this city of billionaires, manual labor still reigns.

Next, visit Mani Bhavan, the house where Gandhi lived from 1917 to 1934 during his Mumbai stays. It was from here that he launched the non-cooperation and civil disobedience movements that changed India's history. The house-museum, preserved in its original state, contains a library of 20,000 volumes, Gandhi's handwritten letters, and period photographs. The atmosphere is sober and contemplative—a striking contrast with the chaos of the street just below.

If you're an early riser and brave, wake at 5 AM for Sassoon Docks—Mumbai's oldest and largest wholesale fish market, founded in 1875. The Koli, the fishermen who are Mumbai's original inhabitants (the name "Mumbai" comes from Mumbadevi, their goddess), unload the day's catch in a frenzy of shouts, crushed ice, and silvery fish. On the warehouse walls, the St+art Foundation has painted giant murals that transform this raw workplace into an open-air art gallery.

Start with Haji Ali Dargah, a 15th-century mosque-mausoleum perched on a rocky islet in the Arabian Sea, connected to the mainland by a 500-meter causeway that vanishes underwater at high tide. The shrine is dedicated to merchant Haji Ali Shah Bukhari, who reputedly abandoned everything after a pilgrimage to Mecca. The atmosphere is powerful: the sea wind, waves licking the causeway, Sufi chants echoing under the white marble dome. Check tide times before going—if the causeway is submerged, you won't be able to access it.

Head next to the CSMVS (Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya, formerly Prince of Wales Museum), an Indo-Saracenic building from 1922 designed by George Wittet—the same architect as the Gateway of India. The collections span 5,000 years of Indian art: Mughal miniatures of extraordinary finesse, Gandhara sculptures (the Greco-Buddhist art of northwest India), weapons, textiles, and archaeological pieces from the Indus Valley Civilization. The palm garden surrounding the museum is a peaceful haven amid the city's din. Allow a good 2 hours.

In the afternoon, venture to Kanheri Caves, in Sanjay Gandhi National Park—104 km² of tropical forest right in Mumbai, an improbable green lung in this megacity. The 109 Buddhist caves, carved from the 1st century BC to the 10th century AD, form one of India's largest rock-cut monastic complexes. Cave 3, called the Great Chaitya, is a 25-meter-long prayer hall with carved pillars and a central stupa. The journey from South Mumbai takes about 1.5 hours—plan a half-day for the round trip and visit.

The return from Nashik to Mumbai (170 km, 3.5 hours) brings you back to the megacity for your final day. Start with a place most tourists miss: Banganga Tank, a 12th-century sacred pool nestled among the skyscrapers of Malabar Hill, one of Mumbai's most expensive neighborhoods. According to legend, the god Rama, thirsty during his journey to Sri Lanka to rescue Sita, shot an arrow that made a tributary of the Ganges spring forth at this spot. The pool, surrounded by small ruined temples and old houses, exudes a village atmosphere frozen in time—200 meters from the glass and steel towers. It's one of Mumbai's best-kept secrets.

Head to Kala Ghoda, Mumbai's arts district. This small area of pedestrian streets and colonial buildings brings together art galleries, independent bookstores, design boutiques, and cafés. The annual Kala Ghoda Festival in February transforms the district into an open-air cultural celebration. Even outside festival season, it's the ideal place to feel the city's creative pulse, far from the clichés of poverty and chaos.

End with Chor Bazaar—literally the "Thieves' Market"—in the Mutton Street neighborhood. This labyrinth of alleyways is Mumbai's largest flea market: antiques, colonial furniture, Bollywood film props, old clocks, gramophones, Art Deco door handles salvaged from demolished buildings. Legend says you can find a stolen object here a few days after losing it. Bargain hard—opening prices are inflated for tourists, but the atmosphere is good-natured.

activities.text: End the day with a sunset stroll along Marine Drive—3 km of seafront curve facing the Arabian Sea, nicknamed the "Queen's Necklace" when the streetlights illuminate at night. The Art Deco buildings from the 1930s-40s lining the promenade form one of the world's largest concentrations of Art Deco architecture, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. What makes this district unique is that these buildings were designed by Indian architects—the first major architectural movement led by Indians during the colonial period. Sit on the concrete parapet with the Mumbaikars, buy bhel puri from a street vendor, and watch the sun plunge into the Arabian Sea.

In the evening, explore the Colaba Causeway district—a shopping street lined with shops, cafés, and restaurants. Dine at one of the city's historic Iranian restaurants, like Leopold Café (open since 1871) or Café Mondegar with its walls painted by caricaturist Mario Miranda. Mumbai's street food is legendary—try a vada pav (the “Mumbai burger”), pav bhaji, or masala dosa from the stalls at Chowpatty Beach.

Returning from Kanheri, if time permits, make a detour through Bandra—Mumbai's "Brooklyn." The Bandra-Worli Sea Link, the 5.6 km cable-stayed bridge spanning the bay, offers spectacular views of Mumbai's skyline. The neighborhood teems with trendy cafés, galleries, and restaurants. The Bandstand Promenade at sunset is a classic.

Before heading to the airport, treat yourself to one last Mumbaikar meal. If you want refined dining, Fort district restaurants offer high-end contemporary Indian cuisine. If you prefer something authentic, one last vada pav from a street stall will be a taste that brings Mumbai flooding back. Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport is 45 minutes to 1.5 hours from South Mumbai depending on traffic—and in Mumbai, traffic is always an unpredictable variable. Allow plenty of time.

visits.text: Descending into Adalaj Vav feels like entering a world with different laws of physics: the temperature drops several degrees as you descend through five levels carved into the rock. Queen Rudabai had this stepwell completed in 1499, deliberately blending Hindu symbols and Islamic geometry on every pillar. Come early in the morning: light filters through the octagonal opening and illuminates the carvings one by one, in sequence.

visits.text: Long drive from Haridwar (about 7 hours). Arrive in Agra early afternoon if you leave early. Drop your things and rush to the Taj Mahal - preferably late afternoon when the golden light sets the white marble ablaze. Shah Jahan had it built between 1632 and 1653 in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died giving birth to their fourteenth child. 20,000 workers and 1,000 elephants labored for 22 years. The central dome rises to 73 meters, and the semi-precious stone inlays (carnelian, lapis lazuli, turquoise, jade) in white marble are mind-blowingly delicate. UNESCO-listed and voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.

2.5 km upstream along the Yamuna, Agra Fort is the city's other jewel. Built in red sandstone by Emperor Akbar from 1565, then embellished in white marble by Shah Jahan, it served as the Mughal imperial residence for generations. This is where Shah Jahan spent his last eight years, imprisoned by his own son Aurangzeb, with only a view of the Taj Mahal he'd built for his wife. From the octagonal tower of Musamman Burj, the view of the Taj is heartbreaking.

Late afternoon, cross the river to Mehtab Bagh ('moonlight garden'), situated directly opposite the Taj Mahal across the Yamuna. It's the best vantage point to photograph the monument at sunset, without the main site's crowds. The garden has been restored and the manicured lawns offer a peaceful setting.

A day devoted to the area around Agra. Start with Fatehpur Sikri (37 km, 45 min), the “city of victory” built by Emperor Akbar between 1571 and 1585 as the new capital of the Mughal Empire. The site has been UNESCO-listed since 1986. Akbar had it built after visiting the Sufi saint Sheikh Salim Chisti, who had predicted the birth of an heir—a prediction that came true. But the city was abandoned after just 14 years, probably due to water shortage. The result: a perfectly preserved red sandstone ghost city, without additions from later centuries.

At Fatehpur Sikri, don't miss the Panch Mahal, a five-story palace entirely open to the winds, built on the Persian windcatcher tower model. The Diwan-i-Khas (Hall of Private Audiences) is famous for its central pillar carved in Gujarati style, from which four walkways branch - Akbar received representatives of different religions here for his famous interfaith debates. Buland Darwaza (Victory Gate), 54 meters high, is one of the world's largest entrance gates.

Within the mosque enclosure, Sheikh Salim Chisti's tomb is a white marble jewel inlaid with jalis (pierced stone screens) of extraordinary delicacy. Childless women come to tie red threads making a wish - the tradition has lasted over four centuries.

Returning toward Agra, stop at Itimad-ud-Daulah's tomb, nicknamed the 'Baby Taj.' Built between 1622 and 1628 by Empress Nur Jahan for her father, it's the first Mughal monument entirely covered in white marble with semi-precious stone inlays - the pietra dura technique that would reach its peak at the Taj Mahal a few years later. The surrounding garden is far less crowded than the Taj and equally photogenic.

activities.text: If you're an early riser, return to the Taj Mahal at dawn - the gates open at sunrise and morning mist over the Yamuna creates an unreal atmosphere. Crowds are much smaller than during the day. This is when professional photographers choose to shoot.

Wander through Kinari Bazaar, Agra's old market near Jama Masjid. Artisans work marble inlaid with semi-precious stones (pietra dura) using the same techniques employed to decorate the Taj Mahal. You'll see workshops open to the street where artisans cut, polish, and inlay by hand.
Taste petha, Agra's signature sweet - a translucent candy made from caramelized white gourd, flavored with rose, saffron, or coconut. Shops around the Taj offer dozens of varieties.

Visit a pietra dura (marble inlay) craft workshop in Agra's artisan quarter. Artisans will show you techniques inherited from Mughal times—cutting, polishing, and inlaying lapis lazuli, malachite, and carnelian in marble. Allow 30 to 45 minutes for a complete demonstration.

If you have time, push on to Akbar's tomb at Sikandra (10 km north of Agra). The emperor who advocated religious tolerance had his own mausoleum designed—an astonishing mix of Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist, and Christian elements. The park is home to herds of deer and troops of langur monkeys.

visits.text: Founded in 1411 by Ahmad Shah on the banks of the Sabarmati River, the old city of Ahmedabad became India's first UNESCO World Heritage City in 2017. Its pols—medieval neighborhoods enclosed by gates—form a labyrinth of houses with carved corbels, communal wells, and shrines tucked between two walls. Arrive early in the morning before the heat settles in; the pol alleyways stand empty before 8am.

Wander through the pols wherever your curiosity takes you: carved wood, the smell of incense, and the cracking sounds of sheep being butchered. Teen Darwaza, the triple Mughal gate facing Bhadra Fort, marks the historic center founded by Ahmad Shah. Look for the bird niches and engraved wells set into the facades—each house tells the story of a caste, a trade, an era. Avoid Sundays: the residents are out.

Step through the gate of Jami Masjid, built in 1424 by Ahmad Shah I according to Gujarat Tourism sources. Two hundred sixty pillars of yellow sandstone carry its domes without a single minaret visible from inside—a deliberate curiosity. The acoustics of the prayer hall amplify the slightest whisper. Enter after Friday prayers to avoid the crowds.

Bhadra Fort seems too small for its history: Ahmad Shah established his first citadel here in 1411, then the Mughals, Marathas, and British succeeded one another, each leaving a layer. Today, merchants flood the central courtyard at dawn. Climb the ramparts for a view over Bhadra Square and Teen Darwaza—two minutes of views over two millennia of accumulated history.

Built in 1848, the Hutheesing Jain Temple is an active temple. Dedicated to the 15th Tirthankara, it stands out for its Kirti Stambha—column of glory—in the center of the courtyard. Admission is free, but shoes must be left at the entrance; visit the interior in silence, as worshippers pray early in the morning.

activities.text: Leave early: the guided Old City Heritage Walk, organized by the municipality, starts at 8am from Swaminarayan Temple. Two hours on foot through the pols with a local guide who knows each facade by its family name. Free registration but places are limited—arrive 15 minutes before the start.

If you have only an hour, Sabarmati Ashram is worth every minute. Gandhi lived here from 1917 to 1930, in a 36-acre house on the banks of the Sabarmati. From here he launched the Salt March in 1930. His spinning wheel, low desk, and thin mattress are visible behind glass. Free entry, open daily.

Manek Chowk market transforms at night into a street-food strip: kebabs, sweets, and steaming chai appear from 10pm where jewelers closed shop at 7pm. The same space serves as a vegetable market at dawn, a jewelers' square by day, and a nighttime restaurant. One square, three daily lives.

visits.text: The descent from Munnar to Alleppey (165 km, 4.5 hours) is as spectacular as the ascent: you leave the tea estates, crossing spice forests, waterfalls, and Tamil villages before returning to the coastal plain. The lower you drop, the more heat and humidity return—brace yourself for the shift. Stop en route for lunch at a "meals" restaurant (local canteen): rice, sambar, rasam, and vegetables served on a banana leaf.

Arriving in Alleppey, board a kettuvallam—these traditional houseboats, 20 to 25 meters long, built from jackwood planks assembled without a single nail, bound with coir rope (coconut fiber), and waterproofed with fish oil. Once used to transport rice from the flooded paddies of Kuttanad, they've been converted into floating accommodations with bedroom, bathroom, and galley. You glide through a labyrinth of coconut-fringed canals, passing fishermen casting nets and children waving from the banks.

Wake on the water—breakfast served on the boat deck, facing the silent morning canals, is one of those moments that alone justify the journey. The morning cruise passes through Kuttanad, nicknamed the "rice bowl of Kerala": it's one of the few places on earth where rice is grown 1.5 to 2 meters below sea level. The FAO has designated this farming system a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System.

After disembarking, explore the village on foot to observe daily life along the canals: coir rope making, fish drying, women in saris washing clothes on the ghats. Locals are welcoming and curious—a smile and a "namaskaram" open every door.

For deeper immersion, board a wooden canoe—these flat-bottomed craft slip into narrow channels where houseboats can't go. You'll glide beneath tunnels of tropical vegetation, threading between water lilies and kingfishers. Count on 1 to 1.5 hours for this silent excursion.

activities.text: Have dinner on board - the cook prepares Keralan dishes with produce bought that very morning in the riverside villages. Karimeen pollichathu (pearl spot grilled in a banana leaf) is the local specialty not to be missed. Watch the sun set from the upper deck as Vembanad Lake - the longest lake in India, 96 km - turns orange and pink. Boats must moor before nightfall so as not to disturb the fishing.

Spend the afternoon birdwatching along the Vembanad banks. Herons, cormorants, egrets, kingfishers—the diversity is remarkable. If you're into photography, the late-afternoon light on the canals offers perfect conditions. Finish the day with a stroll on Alleppey Beach, a long ribbon of golden sand facing the Arabian Sea, often deserted by tourists who stick to the backwaters.

visits.text: A few broken slabs in the grass—and yet the Amaravati site has one of South Asia's longest histories. The Amaravati Stupa, built in several phases between the 3rd century B.C.E. and around 250 C.E. according to Wikipedia, was one of ancient India's largest Buddhist centers. Little remains in place on the site itself: the major sculptures are in the British Museum and the museum in Chennai. The local museum on site displays casts and fragments.

visits.text: You arrive in Amritsar by train (allow around 6 hours from Delhi on the Shatabdi Express). Drop your bags and head straight for the Golden Temple—Harmandir Sahib. It's Sikhism's holiest site, and probably one of the world's most beautiful religious buildings. The temple sits at the center of a sacred pool measuring 150 m by 150 m (the Amrit Sarovar, “pool of nectar”), connected to land by a 60-meter marble causeway. Maharaja Ranjit Singh covered the upper stories with 750 kg of pure gold in the 1830s. Four entrances symbolize openness to all castes and religions. Arrive early in the morning to watch sunrise on the golden dome—the reflection in the water is breathtaking.

Right next to the Golden Temple, push through the narrow gate of Jallianwala Bagh. This is where on April 13, 1919, British General Dyer ordered his troops to fire on an unarmed crowd of thousands gathered for the Baisakhi festival. About 379 dead officially - likely far more. Bullet marks are still visible on the walls, and the well into which dozens jumped to escape the gunfire is preserved. The Flame of Liberty memorial, a 9-meter red sandstone pylon, was inaugurated in 1961. The place is stark and poignant - take time to read the panels.

Don't miss the Partition Museum, housed in Amritsar's old town hall. It traces the 1947 division of India and Pakistan through testimonies, personal objects, and photographs. It's one of the few museums worldwide dedicated to this event, which displaced 15 million people and killed between one and two million.

activities.text: In the late afternoon, drive to the Wagah border (28 km, 45 min). Every evening at sunset, Indian and Pakistani border guards perform the “Beating Retreat” ceremony—a surreal spectacle of high kicks, exaggerated martial postures, and glares, followed by the simultaneous lowering of both flags. 25,000 spectators on the Indian side, a soccer stadium atmosphere. Arrive at least 1 hour 30 minutes before the start to get a good seat.

Eat at the Golden Temple langar - the world's largest free kitchen. Every day over 50,000 meals are prepared and served by volunteers: dal, chapati, vegetables, and kheer. Everyone is welcome, without distinction. Sit in rows on the floor and let yourself be served. The experience is as spiritual as it is gastronomic.

If you return from Wagah in the evening, go back to the Golden Temple at night. The illuminated building is reflected in the pool—it's even more magical than by day. Chants from the Guru Granth Sahib echo in the cool air and devotees circle the pool. A moment of absolute peace after the tumult of the Wagah ceremony.

visits.text: Welcome to Hampi - a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986, this is India's largest field of ruins. In 1500, Vijayanagara was the world's second-largest city after Beijing, with 500,000 inhabitants and merchants from Persia and Portugal. More than 1,600 monuments spread across 42 km² amid a landscape of granite boulders and rice paddies. Allow at least 2.5 days to explore the site.

Start with the Virupaksha Temple, the living heart of Hampi. Dedicated to Shiva, this 7th-century shrine is still in active worship. Its 50-meter gopuram towers over the whole bazaar. Inside, look for the ceiling paintings dating from the 14th and 16th centuries - they depict scenes from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. King Krishnadevaraya added the great pillared hall in 1510 to mark his coronation. Arrive early in the morning: the light is beautiful and the monkeys are still calm.

Then climb Hemakuta Hill, dotted with small Jain and Hindu temples from the 14th and 15th centuries. The real draw is the view: from the top, you take in the whole site on one side and the Tungabhadra on the other. Late in the day, the granite boulders take on an almost unreal golden hue. Settle on the rocks with some water - it is the sunset spot par excellence.

Descend through Hampi Bazaar, the ancient market street in front of Virupaksha. In the 16th century, Portuguese travelers described stalls overflowing with precious stones, spices and Arabian horses. Today, the granite columns that lined the shops still stand - imagine the bustle of this artery at its peak.

Head to Vijaya Vittala Temple, the absolute jewel of Hampi. Begun under Devaraya II (1422-1446) and enriched by Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529), it occupies an enclosure measuring 164 m by 94 m. The star attraction is the Stone Chariot - a stone chariot dedicated to Garuda, inspired by Konark's Sun Temple after Krishnadevaraya discovered it during a campaign in Odisha. The wheels were once mobile, now cemented in place. The complex is open from 8:30am to 5:30pm.

In the Ranga Mantapa, you'll discover the 56 musical pillars nicknamed “SaReGaMa”. Gently tapping each pillar produced sounds like a mridangam, cymbals, or a veena. The British, intrigued, sawed two of them open to unlock the secret - finding nothing inside. The two cut pillars are still visible. Today, touching the pillars is forbidden, but a guard sometimes gives a demonstration.

Continue to the Elephant Stables: 11 aligned domes - some round, others with Islamic cupolas - which housed the royal elephants. It's one of the most striking examples of the empire's Indo-Islamic style. Right next door, the Zenana Enclosure houses the Lotus Mahal, a two-story pavilion whose arches recall an opening lotus flower - a cool retreat designed for the queens.

Make a detour to the Lakshmi Narasimha monolith (6.7 m high), Vishnu in his man-lion form. Push on to Krishna Temple and the Sasivekalu Ganesha - a 2.4 m monolith carved from a single block, named 'mustard seed' for the shape of his belly.

Rise early to climb Anjanadri Hill - the presumed birthplace of the god Hanuman according to the Ramayana. Count on 575 steps (30-40 minutes) between granite blocks. At the summit, a small temple houses a Hanuman idol carved from rock. The real reward is the 360° view: checkered rice paddies, coconut groves, the serpentine Tungabhadra, and all of Hampi spread across the horizon. Go at sunrise. Watch out for monkeys: don't show any food.

Once down, push on to Pampa Sarovar, a sacred basin covered with lotuses - one of Hinduism's five holy lakes. According to legend, this is where the goddess Pampa did penance to marry Shiva. Two small temples border the basin. The place is peaceful and rarely crowded.

Visit Kodandarama Temple on the banks of the Tungabhadra, where Rama is said to have crowned Sugriva king of the monkeys. The bas-reliefs tell the scene with finesse. The setting is magnificent: the river flows just below, lined with water-polished granite blocks.

activities.text: Cross the Tungabhadra in a coracle - these round bamboo boats covered in tar have been used here for centuries. The journey takes 5-10 minutes and drops you on the Anegundi side. The service runs from roughly 7am to 6pm, but depends on water levels (avoid monsoon season). On the Anegundi side, you'll find homestays with views over the rice fields - far more authentic than Hospet.

Set yourself up on the Hemakuta rocks or the north bank for sunset. The granite blocks naturally stacked over billions of years take on orange tones as the sun sinks behind the hills. If you're staying on the Anegundi side, the peace is total - no roads, just the sound of the river.

In the afternoon, rent a bicycle or scooter on the Anegundi side and explore the north bank. You will pass the Gagan Mahal palace (a 16th-century royal residence with Indo-Islamic balconies), the Ranganatha Temple and the ruins of the fort. Artisans still make objects from banana fiber - a local tradition.

Late in the day, descend to Sanapur Lake (4 km from Anegundi): turquoise water between granite blocks, with the possibility of a coracle tour. In the evening, Anegundi is very quiet - perfect for digesting the kilometers of ruins.

Explore the prehistoric rock paintings of Onake Kindi, a few kilometers from Anegundi. These Neolithic paintings testify to human occupation well before the Vijayanagara empire. By scooter, the road through rice paddies and granite chaos is a pleasure.

Organizing departure to Goa: from Hospet Junction (13 km), the Howrah Express departs 4 days/week to Madgaon (7-8 hours). Private overnight buses reach Margao in 8-10 hours. From Margao, count on 40 minutes by bus or taxi to Palolem. Book in advance - berths go fast.

visits.text: Halfway between Vizag and Rajahmundry, Annavaram is known for its Sri Satyanarayana Swamy temple perched on Ratnagiri hill, accessible on foot. The complex offers clear views over the coastal plain and the Pampa River. A brief but worthwhile stop for those who enjoy hilltop temples. Parking at the foot of the hill.

visits.text: The road from Pune to Aurangabad (235 km, 4.5 hours) crosses the Deccan plateau—a landscape of cotton fields, sugarcane, and dusty villages. Aurangabad is your base for the next three days and Maharashtra's two UNESCO jewels: Ajanta and Ellora.

Upon arrival, visit Bibi Ka Maqbara, the mausoleum built in 1660 by Azam Shah, son of Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, in memory of his mother Dilras Banu. It's called the "Poor Man's Taj" or "Taj of the Deccan"—and with good reason: it's an unabashed replica of the Taj Mahal, but executed on a much more modest budget. The base is marble, but the upper portion is stucco painted to imitate marble. The result is both touching and fascinating: same proportions, same Mughal gardens, same symmetry, but a finish that betrays the financial constraints. Far from being a "fake Taj," it's a monument that tells a story of filial love and thwarted ambition.

In the early afternoon, push on to Daulatabad Fort, 15 km from Aurangabad—a 12th-century fortress perched on a 200-meter-high conical hill, considered one of India's most impregnable forts. The craziest story: in 1327, Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq decided to move the entire capital from Delhi here—forcing hundreds of thousands of people to march over 1,000 km across the Deccan. The plan failed miserably and he eventually sent everyone back to Delhi. The climb to the summit passes through dark passages, crocodile moats (now dry), and a spiral tunnel designed to trap invaders in the dark. The view from the top takes in the entire Deccan plateau.

Full day dedicated to Ajanta Caves—plan an early morning departure from Aurangabad (100 km, a 2.5-hour drive). Thirty Buddhist caves carved into the horseshoe-shaped cliff above the Waghora River, UNESCO-listed since 1983. They were excavated in two phases: the first in the 2nd century BC by monks of the Hinayana tradition, the second in the 5th–6th centuries under the Vakatakas, a period of artistic genius without parallel. The caves were abandoned, forgotten, engulfed by jungle for over 1,000 years—until a British officer on a tiger hunt, John Smith, rediscovered them in 1819.

Cave 1 is the absolute masterpiece. The murals—technically tempera on dry plaster, not frescoes—are among the oldest surviving Indian paintings. The Bodhisattva Padmapani, painted on either side of the sanctuary entrance, is Ajanta's most famous image: a being of unsettling beauty, eyes half-closed in compassion, adorned with jewels but his gaze turned inward. The duality between sensuality and spirituality is strikingly modern. Opposite, the Vajrapani, protector wielding the thunderbolt, completes the duo.

Don't miss Cave 17, which preserves the site's most colorful and best-preserved paintings—scenes from the Buddha's life with a vibrancy of color that defies the centuries. Cave 26 houses a 7-meter reclining Buddha, in parinirvana (entering final nirvana), carved from rock with a serenity that stops you dead. Cave 19, a richly decorated chaitya, shows the Buddha in anthropomorphic form—a turning point in Buddhist art.

A mandatory shuttle connects the parking lot to the caves (4 km). The entire site requires 4 to 5 hours to visit. Bring water, a flashlight (the caves are dark), comfortable shoes, and patience—crowds can be heavy in high season. Flash photography is prohibited to protect the paintings. REMINDER: CLOSED MONDAYS.

Spend the whole day at the Ellora caves, just 30 km from Aurangabad. This UNESCO site comprises 34 caves: Buddhist temples (caves 1-12), Hindu temples (caves 13-29) and Jain temples (caves 30-34), carved side by side into the same basalt cliff between the 6th and 11th centuries. This architectural coexistence of three different religions is an exceptional testimony to religious tolerance in ancient India.

The Kailasa Temple (Cave 16) is THE monument that alone justifies the journey. Imagine: an entire temple carved from top to bottom from a single basalt block, starting from the roof and working down—the reverse of conventional construction. The 8th-century architects, under King Krishna I of the Rashtrakuta dynasty, had between 150,000 and 200,000 tonnes of rock extracted to sculpt this temple dedicated to Shiva. The result: a structure 50 meters long, 33 meters wide, and 30 meters high—twice the surface area of Athens' Parthenon. The sculptures adorning the walls—Ravana lifting Mount Kailash, Shiva and Parvati, life-size elephants—have a rare dramatic power. An ancient text from 812 AD reports that the architect himself, upon seeing his completed work, is said to have exclaimed: “How could I have built this?”

Next, explore the Buddhist caves—Cave 10 (Vishvakarma or “Carpenter's Cave”) is a spectacular chaitya with a vault imitating wooden framework. Cave 12 (Teen Tal) is a three-story monastery carved from rock, impressive in its monumental scale. The later Jain caves (30–34) display extraordinarily fine carving—the details of the sculptures and painted ceilings have almost the precision of a jeweler's work.

activities.text: If time allows, detour to Aurangabad Caves—12 Buddhist caves from the 6th-7th centuries, far less known than Ajanta and Ellora but remarkable for their female sculptures of exceptional grace. You'll likely have them all to yourself.

The late afternoon return to Aurangabad is a chance to catch your breath. The road passes through the rural landscapes of Maharashtra's heartland—sorghum fields, buffalo herds, village temples. Dine at one of Aurangabad's restaurants—Marathwada cuisine is robust and spicy, with specialties like naan qalia (spiced lamb) inherited from Mughal cuisine.

Before leaving Ellora, detour to Grishneshwar Temple, 2 km from the caves—one of the 12 Jyotirlinga, Shiva's most sacred temples in India. The current temple dates from the 18th century, but the site has been sacred for much longer. The atmosphere of devotion is intense. REMINDER: Ellora is CLOSED TUESDAYS.

visits.text: Badami boasts four rock-cut temples carved into red sandstone cliffs between the 6th and 8th centuries by the Chalukya dynasty. Cave Temple 1, dedicated to Shiva, is the oldest—you'll see a sculpture of Nataraja (dancing Shiva) displaying 81 codified dance positions. Cave Temple 3, the largest and most impressive, is dedicated to Vishnu and dates to 578 CE—the date is carved in stone. The sculptures are remarkably refined for their era. Wear good shoes—the stairways cut into the rock are steep and slippery.

Below the caves, Agastya Lake forms a turquoise mirror framed by sandstone cliffs. Walk around it (about 30 minutes) to discover small temples and shrines carved into the rock on the opposite shore. If you feel up to it, climb to Badami Fort via the trail starting from the lake's north side—the view from the fort ruins takes in the entire valley and the caves below.

activities.text: Make the most of your day in Badami by taking an excursion to Pattadakal and Aihole, respectively 22 and 34 km away. This Chalukya archaeological triangle is UNESCO-listed (for Pattadakal). At Pattadakal, you'll see about ten temples from the 7th–8th centuries blending Dravidian (southern) and Nagara (northern) styles. Aihole, often called the cradle of Hindu temple architecture, has more than 120 temples scattered across a plateau. Allow half a day for both sites together.

visits.text: If you're arriving from Puducherry by overnight bus or car (around 5-6 hours via NH77/NH44), you'll arrive at Majestic bus terminal right in the heart of Bengaluru. Take advantage of this stop to arrange your bus or train tickets to Hampi - Kempegowda bus station is Karnataka's main hub, with daily KSRTC buses departing for Hospet (7-8 hours by road). Book the day before if you're traveling during peak season (October-February).

Cubbon Park is Bengaluru's green lung: 120 hectares of gardens created in 1870 by General Sankey, with over 6,000 trees - from gulmohar with brilliant red flowers to imposing silver oaks. You'll also find the State Central Library, a superb red-painted Gothic building, and the Government Museum, one of India's oldest (founded in 1876). If you're there on a Sunday, the park is closed to cars and transforms into a venue for yoga, concerts and a small farmers' market.

Right next to the park, don't miss Vidhana Soudha: this massive neo-Dravidian building, constructed in 1954, houses Karnataka's parliament. You can't go inside, but the illuminated granite facade in the evening is worth a detour. Opposite, Attara Kacheri (1864) with its Corinthian columns houses the High Court - a striking contrast between colonial architecture and Indian style.

activities.text: Stroll down MG Road, Bengaluru's historic shopping artery. It's less about the shopping than the atmosphere - trendy cafes, bookshops and old-school stores coexist in a distinctly Bangalorean energy. If you're hungry, head to VV Puram Food Street (3 km south) to sample crispy dosas and fluffy bondas.

Preparing for departure to Hampi: from Majestic, overnight KSRTC buses depart between 8pm and 10pm for Hospet (arriving around 6-7am). If you prefer the train, the Hampi Express (#16592) leaves Bengaluru at 10pm and arrives at Hospet Junction around 7:10am. From there, it's 13 km by auto-rickshaw to the ruins. Take a sleeper bus or train berth to sleep en route and save a day.

visits.text: In Betul, you visit Balajipuram temple in Betul Bazar. Its architecture follows the forms of South Indian temples. Sculpted figures and pictures in the complex depict episodes from Rama's life. This religious stop is close to the town for this stage of the route, between the central jungles and the archaeological treasures of Madhya Pradesh.

activities.text: You stop in Betul to explore the Satpura plateau on foot or by car. The teak forests and views over the surrounding valleys are worth an hour of wandering.

visits.text: Telugus call it Dakshina Ayodhya—the Ayodhya of the South. Sri Sita Rama Temple of Bhadrachalam, dedicated to Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana, was built in 1630 by Kancherla Gopanna, a royal tax collector turned saint and poet. Legend says he financed the temple with the sultan's taxes, was imprisoned for it, and that Rama himself appeared to repay the debt. On the banks of the Godavari, the atmosphere is that of a living pilgrimage.

activities.text: If you pass through in March–April for Sita Rama Kalyanam, the celestial wedding ceremony of Rama and Sita is broadcast live throughout Andhra and Telangana. The crowd is immense, but the collective emotion is palpable. Outside the festival, evenings on the banks of the Godavari remain a quiet time to observe river life.

visits.text: Eight sanctuaries cut into the rock about a thousand years ago, each dedicated to a different form of Shiva: the Bhairavakona temples are hewn straight into the cliff face in the Nallamala hills. Local legend holds that no crow ever enters the valley—and visitors confirm it. An unusual detail: on Karthika Pournami (the November full moon), moonlight falls directly onto the deity in the main cave.

The water falls into a natural pool surrounded by jungle: pilgrims bathe at Bhairavakona waterfall before entering the temples. According to local tradition, the water flows through medicinal plants in the hills. The view is better from October to January, when the flow is strong. Free entry.

days_plan.itin_title: India's East Coast: Chennai to Visakhapatnam, 13 Days

visits.text: Thirty thousand years of humanity on sandstone walls—Bhimbetka isn't a museum, it's raw continuity. More than 700 shelters carved by wind in the Vindhya hills, 400 of them covered with rock paintings ranging from the Paleolithic to the Middle Ages. UNESCO-listed in 2003. Archaeologist V.S. Wakankar discovered the site in 1957 by chance, from a train. Fifteen shelters are open to the public.

Archaeologist V.S. Wakankar discovered Bhimbetka in 1957 by glimpsing the sandstone outcrops from a train. What he found is South Asia's largest collection of prehistoric rock art—depictions of aurochs, deer, hunting scenes, and rituals that trace human evolution from hunter-gatherer to farmer. Australia has Kakadu, France has Lascaux, India has Bhimbetka.

activities.text: If you arrive when the site opens at 7am, the 15 shelters along the route are deserted and the sandstone forest is still cool. The silence combined with the paintings creates a sense of time that is hard to find elsewhere. Avoid weekends and public holidays. A local guide knows where to find the best paintings, which are not signposted.

visits.text: A temple unfinished since the 11th century—yet with strikingly powerful forms. Bhojeshwar Temple of Bhojpur, built by Raja Bhoj of the Paramara dynasty between 1010 and 1055, houses one of India's largest shivalingas: 5.5 meters tall, carved from a single block of stone. The dome was never installed. You can still see the earth ramps of medieval stonemasons and architectural plans carved on nearby rocks.

activities.text: The 11th-century stonemasons carved their own architectural plans directly onto the flat rocks around the temple—pillars, moldings, cross-sections. It's the equivalent of a stone construction notebook, unique in medieval Indian architecture. Look for these engravings east of the temple, on the ground.

days_plan.itin_title: From Coast to Jungle: Bhubaneswar to Bhopal in 16 Days

visits.text: Bhongir Fort looks as though it has been placed on a giant egg: the 50-acre oval monolithic rock on which it perches is perfectly isolated. It was built in 1076 by the Chalukya king Tribhuvanamalla Vikramaditya VI, hence its original name, Tribhuvanagiri. The 500-foot climb takes 30 minutes; the view over the Deccan plain on the way down is worth every step.

days_plan.itin_title: Deccan: Bahmani Sultans and Kakatiya Temples in 12 Days

visits.text: India's largest mosque deserves a visit even if you're not a believer. Bhopal's Taj-ul-Masajid, literally "Crown of Mosques," was commissioned in the 19th century by Nawab Shah Jahan Begum and can accommodate roughly 175,000 worshippers in its courtyard. Three white domes and two pink minarets dominate the old city. Free entry. Closed to non-Muslims on Fridays.

Bhopal's Upper Lake, created in the 11th century by Raja Bhoja of the Paramara dynasty, is India's oldest artificial lake still in operation. It spans 31 km². Ramsar site. Sair Sapata, a leisure complex on its shores, offers paddle boats and a musical fountain—family-friendly, lively, very Indian.

If you have time in late afternoon, Van Vihar National Park, on the edge of Upper Lake, is a zoo in semi-natural enclosures: tigers, lions, leopards, and bears behind simple barriers, in greenery. Entry by car or on foot. A gentle way to close a road trip through jungles.

activities.text: Bhopal's old city smells of kebab and naan bread fresh from the tandoor. The Chowk quarter, below Taj-ul-Masajid, is packed with Muslim pastry shops, spice merchants, and suit tailors. An hour walking here with no particular aim is worth any official tour.

Bhopalis swear by morning poha-jalebi: flattened rice sautéed with onions and chilies, served with a sweet jalebi soaked in syrup. It makes no sense in theory but is excellent in practice. Look for a counter open from 7am on streets near the railway station.

days_plan.itin_title: From Coast to Jungle: Bhubaneswar to Bhopal in 16 Days

visits.text: Train from Kolkata to Bhubaneswar (about 7 hours on the Shatabdi). The 'city of a thousand temples' closes this circuit with a return to Indian spirituality's roots. Lingaraj Temple, Bhubaneswar's largest and most venerated, dates from the 11th century. Its 55-meter tower (deul) dominates the city - it's the finest example of Kalinga architectural style. Entry is reserved for Hindus, but you can observe the temple from a raised platform outside the enclosure, originally installed for Lord Curzon.

Rajarani Temple (11th century) is nicknamed the “love temple” for its sculptures of entwined couples and celestial nymphs recalling Khajuraho, on a smaller scale. Unlike Lingaraj, it's open to all. The surrounding garden is peaceful—the sandstone sculptures, turned golden by the late afternoon light, are magnificent.

Visit Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves, carved in the 2nd century BC by King Kharavela to house Jain monks. Udayagiri ('sunrise hill') has 18 caves adorned with detailed bas-reliefs showing court scenes and elephant processions. Rani Gumpha ('queen's cave'), on two levels, is the most spectacular. Khandagiri, opposite, offers a panoramic view over Bhubaneswar from its summit.

If you have time, detour to Dhauli (8 km south), where Emperor Ashoka, after the bloody Battle of Kalinga in 261 BC that killed over 100,000, had a crisis of conscience that converted him to Buddhism. The rock edicts of Ashoka carved in stone are among India's oldest texts. The white Shanti Stupa (Peace Stupa), built in 1972 by the Japanese at the hilltop, offers unobstructed views over rice paddies.

activities.text: Explore Ekamra Haat market, a permanent craft market where Odisha artisans display their specialties: stone carvings, patachitra (paintings on canvas), Cuttack silver filigree jewelry, and ikat fabrics. It's the ideal spot for quality souvenirs at reasonable prices.

Taste Odisha cuisine: dalma (lentils with vegetables and coconut), pakhala bhata (rice fermented in water - Odisha's emblematic dish, served cold), and chhena poda (caramelized fresh cheese cake), a specialty unavailable elsewhere in India.

visits.text: Aina Mahal confounds: Venetian mirrors, mechanical fountains, Dutch earthenware, and court sculptures—all commissioned in 1761 by Rao Lakhpatji from Ram Singh Malam, a Gujarati craftsman trained in Europe for seventeen years. The 2001 earthquake damaged the palace; traces of cracks remain visible in some rooms. Visiting hours 9am–11:45am and 3pm–5:45pm; closed Friday.

Prag Mahal, designed in 1865 by British architect Henry Saint Clair Wilkins for Maharao Pragmalji II, rises as a neo-Gothic tower in the heart of Kutch. Italian marble, crystal chandeliers, a durbar hall with a vaulted ceiling: the building is more unexpected than an ordinary Rajput palace. Climb the clock tower for a view over the city.

activities.text: Bhuj's bazaar smells of sesame oil and tanned leather: repoussé copper, painted leather belts, banjara embroidery, and ajrakh textiles pile up in shops opening onto the lane. Bhujodi Village, 10 km away, is the hub of Kutchi weavers—quieter and easier to navigate. Go in the afternoon when workshops are active.

days_plan.itin_title: Gujarat: Grand Tour of UNESCO Sites in 15 Days

visits.text: Rebuilt in 1428 by Ahmad Shah Bahmani when he shifted his capital from Gulbarga, Bidar Fort crowns a red laterite cliff. Triple moat 9 meters deep, 37 bastions, and inside: Rangin Mahal, whose Persian mosaics have weathered six centuries of warfare. Open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Mahmud Gawan's madrasa looks like Samarkand transported to the Deccan. Built in 1472 by this Persian merchant turned Prime Minister, it housed 3,000 manuscripts in its library. One of two minarets survived the 1696 gunpowder explosion. The remaining turquoise faience tiles are enough to grasp what once was.

Continue to Ashtur for the Bahmani Tombs, a cluster of royal mausoleums—some double-storied—scattered across a dusty field 3 km from town. No official guides on-site; ask the caretakers, who know each tomb by name.

activities.text: Brass gleams in Bidar's workshops: artisans practice bidriware, a technique of silver inlay on zinc-copper alloy dating back to the Bahmani era. A workshop near the fort sells directly. Allow 20 minutes to watch the process—drawing, hammering, inlaying—before purchasing.

days_plan.itin_title: Deccan: Bahmani Sultans and Kakatiya Temples in 12 Days

visits.text: The Gol Gumbaz in Bijapur (now Vijayapura) has an unsupported dome with an internal diameter of 37.9 meters. The building was constructed in 1656 as the mausoleum of Sultan Mohammed Adil Shah, and its whispering gallery at the base of the dome amplifies the slightest sound dramatically—a whisper on one side can be heard clearly at the other end, 37 meters away. Climb the spiral staircase (seven stories) to reach the gallery and enjoy panoramic views of the city. Mind your ears—the noise can be deafening when school groups shout inside.

One kilometer west, don't miss Ibrahim Rauza, often compared to a miniature Taj Mahal. This mausoleum and its adjoining mosque were built between 1615 and 1627 for Ibrahim Adil Shah II. The proportions are remarkably elegant, with finely carved arches, delicate minarets, and calligraphic stone inscriptions. Legend has it that Shah Jahan drew inspiration from it when designing the Taj Mahal. The site is much less crowded than Gol Gumbaz—take the opportunity to take your time.

activities.text: Bijapur deserves some aimless wandering through its lanes: the citadel ramparts (6.5 km perimeter), Jami Masjid mosque with its 2,250 prayer spaces, and the numerous tombs and pavilions of the Adil Shahi sultans are scattered throughout the city. Rent an auto-rickshaw by the hour to cover the more distant sites. Late in the day, sunset from the ramparts is a welcome moment of calm after a day of sightseeing.

days_plan.itin_title: South India Circuit: Temples, Backwaters & Wellness

visits.text: Drive from Varanasi (250 km, about 5 hours). Bodhgaya is Buddhism's holiest site—this is where Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment under a sacred fig tree (pipal) about 2,500 years ago, becoming the Buddha. The Mahabodhi Temple, UNESCO-listed since 2002, marks this exact spot. The 55-meter pyramidal tower, rebuilt between the 5th and 6th centuries, dominates the site. Behind the temple, the descendant of the original Bodhi tree still stands—you'll see monks from all Buddhist traditions meditating at its feet, from Tibetans in purple robes to Thais in orange robes.

Tour the international monasteries surrounding Mahabodhi Temple—each Buddhist country has built its own in its own architectural style. The Thai monastery with its golden roof, the minimalist Japanese temple, the colorful Tibetan monastery, the Chinese temple, and the Burmese temple offer a Buddhist world tour in a single walk. The whole tour covers about 2 km and is easily done on foot.

The Great Buddha Statue (25 meters tall), inaugurated in 1989 by the Dalai Lama, sits in a Japanese garden south of the main temple. It depicts Buddha in meditation posture, seated on a lotus - the 10 smaller statues at the base represent his principal disciples.

activities.text: Join a guided meditation session at one of the monasteries - several offer free sessions for visitors, usually in the morning. The experience of meditating at the very place where Buddha attained Enlightenment has particular resonance, whether you're Buddhist or not.

In the evening, return to Mahabodhi Temple for evening prayers. Monks light hundreds of lamps around the temple and Bodhi tree - the atmosphere is deeply calm. The contrast with Varanasi's frenetic energy is total.

visits.text: Raniji ki Baori is the largest of Bundi's 50 stepwells—and one of Rajasthan's most impressive. Built in 1699 by Queen Nathavati Ji Solanki, it plunges 46 meters deep. You enter on the second level through an arched portal flanked by marble elephant statues. Each level houses a place of worship, and the pillars are carved with figures of Vishnu—look for his incarnations as Varaha (boar), Matsya (fish) and Narasimha (man-lion). The entrance is small and easy to miss on the main street.

The Garh Palace seems to emerge from the cliff face—seen from below, the effect is striking. Built by Rao Raja Ratan Singh between 1607 and 1631, it's renowned for its turquoise and gold frescoes of the Bundi miniature painting school, created with natural pigments (minerals, vegetables, precious stones, silver and gold). Enter through the Hathi Pol (Elephant Gate), climb to the Diwan-e-Aam, then push on to the Chhatra Mahal and Badal Mahal. Warning: many rooms are closed and left to the bats—a flashlight is useful.

Taragarh Fort (Star Fort) crowns the hill above Garh Palace. Built in the 14th century, it offers a panoramic view over Bundi, its blue houses and the Aravalli. The climb is steep—bring good shoes and water. At the top: labyrinthine passages, crumbling bastions and rock-cut reservoirs. No infrastructure, no crowds—raw Rajasthan.

Bundi resembles a miniature Jodhpur, minus the tourists. Blue houses, narrow lanes and vintage shops evoke another century. Wander through the fruit and vegetable market in the town center, where merchants wear imposing colorful turbans. This is also where Rudyard Kipling reportedly found inspiration for Kim—he stayed at Sukh Mahal, a small palace on the edge of Jait Sagar lake.

activities.text: Set out to discover Bundi's hidden baoris—the town once had about a hundred. Dhabhai Kund, not far from Raniji ki Baori, is a massive 17th-century symmetrical well—possibly India's second largest. Also seek out Nagar Sagar Kund, twin wells near Chougan Gate, often overlooked amid the bustle of the shops.

days_plan.itin_title: Intensive Rajasthan Road Trip: Forts, Tigers & Taj Mahal

visits.text: Archaeologists call it “the only intact pre-Mughal Islamic city in India”—and UNESCO listed Champaner-Pavagadh in 2004. The ruins of this former capital of the Gujarat Sultanate under Mahmud Begada in the 15th century extend over several kilometers: gates, palaces, mosques, wells, and granaries. Pavagadh mountain, which overlooks the site, has been home to Jain and Hindu temples since the 8th century.

Champaner's Jami Masjid alone justifies the stop: its six-story minarets, colonnaded courtyards, and carved mashrabiyas fuse Hindu and Islamic architecture in a balance that exists nowhere else. Built in the late 15th century, the edifice is well-preserved and little visited.

activities.text: If you have the energy, ascend to Kalikamata temple at the summit of Pavagadh by cable car, then continue up the steps on foot—the view over the Gujarat plain is unbeatable. Dedicated to the goddess Kali, the temple is a major Shakti Peetha visited by Hindu pilgrims throughout the year. Combined with Champaner below, the site easily fills half a day.

days_plan.itin_title: Gujarat: Grand Tour of UNESCO Sites in 15 Days

visits.text: Chandigarh is a transit stop between Manali and Rishikesh (307 km from Manali, about 6 hours 35 minutes by road). But the city is worth a stop: it's the only Indian city planned by Le Corbusier in the 1950s, after Partition. The Capitol Complex, UNESCO-listed in 2016, brings together the High Court, Secretariat, and Assembly—a monumental complex of raw concrete that is surprising in the Indian context. The Open Hand, a 26-meter-tall sculpture, turns freely with the wind and symbolizes peace.

Do not miss the Rock Garden, the work of one man - Nek Chand, a roads inspector who secretly built a sculpture garden from recycled urban waste (pottery fragments, construction rubble, broken bangles) on 16 hectares of government land. Discovered in 1975, the site faced demolition, but public support saved it. The mosaic figures lined up by the hundreds create a striking visual effect.

If you have an hour free, walk along Sukhna Lake, an artificial lake created in 1958 by building a dam across a seasonal stream. Locals take their evening stroll here, and boats are available. The late-day light on the water with the Shivaliks in the background is superb.

activities.text: Take a tour of Sector 17, Chandigarh's pedestrian shopping center, designed by Le Corbusier. The arcades and plazas recall a European city transplanted to India. It's a good place to eat - Punjabi cuisine here is among the country's best.

Visit the Rose Garden (Zakir Hussain Rose Garden), which spreads over 12 hectares and houses more than 1,600 rose varieties. It's Asia's largest rose garden - and in season (February-March), the spectacle is enchanting.

visits.text: Built as early as 1640, Fort St. George is the first English fortress in India—and it's still standing, intact, at the heart of the modern city. The fort houses a museum with weapons, uniforms, coins, and manuscripts from the East India Company era. Enter before 10 a.m. to avoid school groups; on Fridays, the Legislative Assembly is in session and certain wings close.

The scent of incense and jasmine drifts from the stalls before you even glimpse the gopuram of Kapaleeshwarar Temple. This Shiva temple in the Mylapore quarter is said to have been founded two millennia ago, then considerably expanded under the Vijayanagara kings in the 16th century. The entrance tower, covered in multicolored sculptures, ranks among Chennai's finest examples of Dravidian architecture. Come out shoes in hand: the ground burns at midday.

Not glamorous at first glance, the Government Museum of Chennai turns out to be one of India's oldest, with collections spanning the Chola, Hoysala, and Vijayanagara dynasties. The 9th–11th-century Chola bronzes alone justify the trip. Allow three to four hours; separate ticket for the National Art Gallery.

You walk along thirteen kilometers of golden sand on Marina Beach, the world's second-longest urban beach according to most sources. Crowded late in the day with families, vendors selling fried snacks, and cricket players. The stretch between the lighthouse and Foreshore Estate is calmer. Avoid swimming in any season: the currents are dangerous.

Syrian Christians call it the world's third basilica built over an apostle's tomb—alongside St. Peter's in Rome and the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela. San Thome Cathedral Basilica was erected by the Portuguese in 1504 over the burial site of Thomas the Apostle, who arrived in India in 52 A.D. according to tradition. The current neo-Gothic edifice dates from 1893–1896. Descend into the crypt to see the tomb; the adjacent small museum displays relics. Closed in the early afternoon on weekdays.

You enter Kapaleeshwarar Temple through the great side gate to see the inner courtyard, often less photographed than the gopuram. This is where the morning ceremonies unfold between 5 a.m. and 10 a.m.: drumming, incense smoke, devotees in white saris. Arrive early if you want to witness the rituals without the afternoon crowds.

activities.text: If you reach Mylapore's flower market before 7 a.m., you'll see Chennai at its best: jasmine and marigold wholesalers, ox-drawn carts, tea served in steel tumblers. The market empties fast once the sun rises. Plan forty-five minutes on-site.

Chaotic on the surface, the Marina Beach fishing harbor reveals its own rhythm at dawn: catamarans returning fully loaded, fish being sorted on the sand, the smell of salt and diesel. A free, raw spectacle—wear sturdy shoes and be prepared to brave it.

Mylapore on foot in the evening is the real Chennai: flower vendors, cafés serving filter coffee in steel tumblers, Kanjivaram silk shops open until 10 p.m. The neighborhood has kept its 17th-century network of streets around the temple tank. Start at the Kapali tank and wander without a map.

visits.text: Chittorgarh Fort is India's largest fort: 280 hectares enclosed by 4.5 km of ramparts, perched 180 meters above the plains. A UNESCO site since 2013, it has seven successive gates—Padan Pol, Bhairon Pol, Hanuman Pol, Ganesh Pol, Jorla Pol, Laxman Pol and Ram Pol—which you'll pass through driving up. The site contains 65 structures including 4 palaces, 19 temples and 2 towers. Around 3,000 people still live within the walls.

Rana Kumbha Palace, the most massive of the fort's ruins, has foundations dating back to 734 under Bappa Rawal. Rebuilt by Maharana Kumbha in the 15th century, the palace is said to be the birthplace of Maharana Udai Singh—saved as a baby by his nursemaid Panna Dai, who reportedly hid him in a fruit basket to protect him from a usurper. The remains still show stables, water reservoirs and women's quarters (zenana). It's also the site of the terrible jauhars—the collective self-immolations of Rajput women facing invading armies.

You will see the Vijay Stambha (Victory Tower) from afar—37 meters of red sandstone and white marble, 9 stories, 157 steps. Built between 1442 and 1449 by Rana Kumbha to celebrate his victory over the Sultan of Malwa.

Smaller at 22 meters but older, the Kirti Stambha (Tower of Fame) dates from the 12th century. Dedicated to Adinath, the first Jain master, it's adorned with Jain sculptures across its entire surface. The 54 steps lead to the top via a very narrow staircase—claustrophobics beware. It testifies to the religious coexistence that prevailed in the fort.

Make a detour to the Mirabai Temple, built in classic north Indian style. It commemorates the famous 16th-century mystic poet, a Krishna devotee whose fervor scandalized the royal court. The small sanctuary surrounded by an open porch with four pavilions has a soothing atmosphere after the intensity of the ruins of war.

activities.text: Take a tuk-tuk or private vehicle to complete the full circuit of the fort—at 280 hectares, covering it on foot in a day is impossible. Allow 3 to 4 hours to link the palaces, towers and temples, photo stops included.
If you stay into evening, the sound and light show recounts the battles and jauhars of the fort under the stars. Timings vary by season—check on-site.

visits.text: Train from Ernakulam Junction to Coimbatore Junction - about 3.5 hours, with departures roughly every 4 hours. The journey runs along the Western Ghats with beautiful views of tropical vegetation. On arrival, Coimbatore is an industrial city with little tourist charm, but it's the gateway to the Nilgiris and Isha Yoga Center.

Head to Isha Yoga Center, 30 km west of Coimbatore, at the foot of the Velliangiri mountains. The Adiyogi statue greets you: 34 meters high (112 feet), 45 meters long - it's the world's largest sculpted bust according to Guinness. Inaugurated in 2017, its height symbolizes the 112 pathways to liberation in yogic tradition. Entry is free.

Inside the complex, the Dhyanalinga is a unique meditation space - a dome of 250,000 bricks built without steel or cement, housing a consecrated linga. Whatever your beliefs, sit for a few minutes in the dome's silence. Sound offerings (chanting and Tibetan bowls) take place at 11:50am and 5:50pm. The Linga Bhairavi Temple, dedicated to the divine feminine aspect, is right next door.

activities.text: Every evening at 7pm, the Adiyogi Divya Darshanam sound and light show projects a 14-minute light fresco onto the giant statue, telling the story of yoga - it's visually impressive. Note: mobile phones are not allowed in the complex (lockers at the entrance).

If you want to go deeper, the center offers guided meditation sessions and baths in the Theerthakunds - Surya Kund (men) and Chandra Kund (women), consecrated water pools. The complex also has accommodation (cottages, dormitories) if you want to spend the night - but book ahead.

visits.text: Day in the Nilgiris: climb to Coonoor (70 km, 2 hours of winding road from Coimbatore) - the second-largest hill station in the Nilgiris after Ooty, perched at 1,800 m altitude. The road climbs through eucalyptus and shola forests (high-altitude tropical forests) with hairpin bends. If you can, take the Nilgiri Mountain Railway (UNESCO heritage) from Mettupalayam - the rack railway climbs through tea plantations. Book ahead.

Dolphin's Nose is a natural viewpoint perched at 1,550 meters, about thirty minutes by road from Coonoor - a rocky spur shaped like a dolphin's nose. On a clear day, the view takes in the valleys, tea plantations as far as the eye can see and, in the distance, Catherine Falls. The road there runs through kilometers of tea gardens - stop to photograph the pickers in colorful saris between the rows of tea bushes.

Highfield Tea Factory offers a guided tour of the tea-making process, from picking to drying. You'll see the rolling machines, oxidation vats and dryers. At the end, a tasting lets you compare white, green and black teas from the Nilgiris. The shop also sells eucalyptus oil and artisan chocolate. Open 9am to 7pm.

Today you're sleeping at altitude. From Coonoor (where you were yesterday for Dolphin's Nose and Highfield Tea Factory), take the Nilgiri Mountain Railway between Coonoor and Ooty - 19 km of UNESCO-listed rack railway, pulled by diesel locomotive through tea plantations and shola forests. The train passes through Wellington, Lovedale and Ketti before arriving in Ooty (Udhagamandalam) at 2,200 m altitude. The full Mettupalayam-Ooty route (46 km) takes 5 hours and crosses 16 tunnels and 250 bridges - it's India's only rack railway, built by the British and opened in 1899. Book your tickets in advance, especially in season (October-June).

In Ooty, visit the Government Botanical Gardens - 22 hectares of gardens founded in 1848 by the British, with a collection of over 1,000 plant species including fossilized trees 20 million years old. The terraced garden descends along a hillside, with a rose section, fern house and massive tropical trees. Allow 1-1.5 hours to visit. Entry is modest.

Head back down to Coonoor at the end of the day, by train or by road. On the way or once there, stop at Sim's Park - a 12-hectare botanical garden nestled in a natural ravine, with species of pine, magnolia and trees endemic to the Nilgiris. The park is less crowded than the Ooty gardens and makes for a very pleasant walk in hilly surroundings.

activities.text: Multiple photo stops along the Nilgiris road - Lamb's Rock offers a plunging view over the Coimbatore plains and forests below. Monkeys are numerous and bold: keep your belongings in hand. Sim's Park (12 hectares of botanical garden) is also worth a visit if you have time.

Late in the day, instead of descending to Coimbatore, stay at altitude in Coonoor - accommodation is plentiful, from colonial homestays to resorts with valley views. The nighttime coolness (15°C) is a luxury after days in the southern heat. Tomorrow, you'll explore Ooty by rack railway before descending.

In the morning, trek to Droog Fort - an old military outpost of Tipu Sultan (18th century) perched at 1,800 m altitude, 15 km from Coonoor. Only a wall and watchtower remain, but the path crossing Nonsuch Estate's tea plantations (3-4 km walk) is superb. From the summit, the view plunges over the entire Coonoor valley. Watch for wild bison in the area - keep your distance. Bring good shoes and water, there's nothing at the top.

Evening in Coonoor: the cool altitude (15-20°C at night) is a welcome relief after the plains' heat. Enjoy a masala chai in one of the small shops in Coonoor bazaar, or try the artisan chocolates and local fruit jams - the region is known for its high-altitude products. Bring a sweater for the evening.

visits.text: The Little Rann of Kutch covers 4,953 km² - a semi-arid salt desert housing the Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary. It is home to the Indian wild ass, the ghudkhar, a fast animal capable of outrunning predators. The sanctuary also shelters jackals, hyenas and nilgai. Closed during the monsoon (mid-June to mid-October), when the plain is flooded.

activities.text: A safari here is unlike any other: no dense vegetation, no hides. Just the white horizon of salt pans and silhouettes that emerge. Ghudkhars live in herds led by a stallion—you spot them by their dark dorsal stripes. Book a jeep safari through local resorts in Dasada or Zainabad; morning outings (before 8am) are most productive between October and March.

Pink dawn over the salt marshes: flamingos take off by the hundreds from Nawa Talao lake near Dasada. The Little Rann hosts over 250 species of resident and migratory birds, including demoiselle cranes and steppe buzzards in winter. Bring binoculars—distances here are deceptive.

days_plan.itin_title: Gujarat: Grand Tour of UNESCO Sites in 15 Days

visits.text: Dharamsala is about 5 hours by road from Amritsar—the road gradually climbs toward the Himalayan foothills. Your destination is McLeod Ganj, “little Lhasa,” perched at an altitude of 1,770 m. The Dalai Lama has lived here since 1959, after fleeing Chinese-occupied Tibet. Begin with the Tsuglagkhang complex, the spiritual heart of the Tibetan community in exile. The main temple houses a 3-meter golden statue of Buddha Shakyamuni, flanked by Avalokiteshvara and Padmasambhava. The atmosphere is peaceful—monks in crimson robes, prayer wheels spinning, whispers of mantras.

Right next door, the Kalachakra Temple contains frescoes depicting the 722 deities of the mandala, painted over three years by three master painters under the Dalai Lama's personal direction. Photography is forbidden, but the level of detail in the mandalas is stunning.

Visit the Tibet Museum at Gangchen Kyishong in Dharamsala, within the Central Tibetan Administration complex. It traces the history of Tibet as an independent nation, Chinese occupation since 1949, and exile. The testimonies of political prisoners and archival photographs are deeply moving. Allow at least 45 minutes.

Walk down to Namgyal Monastery, the Dalai Lama's personal monastery, founded in 1564. If you're there around 1:30pm (except Sundays), you can watch the monks' debates in the courtyard - a fascinating spectacle where arguments are punctuated with theatrical hand-clapping. The monks are usually delighted to chat with visitors.

activities.text: Walk to Bhagsu Waterfall, about 2 km from McLeod Ganj. The walk passes through Bhagsu village and climbs among rocks toward the waterfall. Bring walking shoes. At the top, several cafés with valley views serve momos (Tibetan dumplings) and butter tea.

Wander McLeod Ganj's lanes - Tibetan shops sell singing bowls, thangkas (fabric paintings), woolen shawls, and turquoise jewelry. Cafés serve authentic Tibetan cuisine: thukpa (noodle soup), steamed or fried momos, and the famous yak butter tea. A world apart from the Indian plains.
Take a thangka painting or Tibetan cooking class—several centers in McLeod Ganj offer half-day workshops. It's a hands-on way to connect with Tibetan culture beyond superficial tourism.

visits.text: Nothing to see here, you think upon arriving at this salt island. Then the excavations appear: streets laid out with precision, water reservoirs, a citadel. Dholavira is one of the largest known Harappan cities, occupied between 3000 and 1500 BCE. Listed by UNESCO in 2021, it stretches over 100 hectares on Khadir Bet island, in the Great Rann of Kutch. A signboard with ten Harappan letters discovered here is the oldest example of writing on a signboard found at sites of the Indus civilization.

Discovered during excavations launched in 1967–68, Dholavira's archaeological museum brings together pottery, copper tools, measuring instruments, and stone ornaments. It helps explain the site's seven phases of occupation—from its peak to abandonment, then reoccupation with a noticeably impoverished culture. Open 9am–5pm, closed Friday.

activities.text: Visit Dholavira's archaeological museum before touring the main site—the context provided makes the ruins easier to understand. Bring water (no shops on site) and a hat: the sun beats down mercilessly on the white stones. The access road is long and isolated; aim to arrive in the early afternoon so you can leave before dark.

visits.text: Salt crunches underfoot. On the horizon, the white of the Great Rann of Kutch merges with the white of the sky, with no clear boundary between them. Dhordo is the gateway village to the salt desert and the starting point of Rann Utsav, a cultural festival organized by Gujarat Tourism between November and March. Outside the festival, the desert is accessible with an entry permit (rannpermit.gujarat.gov.in). Sunset over the salt flats is unlike anything else.

activities.text: If the full moon coincides with your visit to the Great Rann, plan to spend the night here: the white desert under a full moon is one of the strangest panoramas on the subcontinent. Rann Utsav offers evenings of music and crafts at Dhordo's official tent city, with Kutchi embroidery, bandhani, and mirror work. Reservations are necessary in high season (December–February).

Head down to Dhordo village in the morning to meet the Rabari and Mutwa communities, pastoral nomads whose mirror embroidery stands out at first glance. The village hosted the first G20 tourism working group in 2023. Artisan women sell direct; prices are negotiated face-to-face.

visits.text: Built between 1535 and 1541 by Dom Nuno da Cunha after the defeat of the Sultan of Gujarat, Diu Fort watches over the island's eastern tip from its double moat filled with seawater. Its 20-meter walls, 22 cannons, and interior tunnels are in good condition. The Portuguese remained until Operation Vijay in 1961—426 years of presence visible in every stone.

St. Paul's Church defies categories: Portuguese Baroque on the Indian coast, built between 1601 and 1610, with angels, vines, and horsemen depicted in its carved wood that owe more to Lisbon than to Ahmedabad. Still active. Nearby, St. Thomas Church has become Diu Museum—colonial artifacts, marquetry, and nautical charts.

activities.text: Diu's lanes smell of dried fish and cold beer—a rarity in Gujarat, where alcohol is prohibited. The island is a Union Territory, so Gujarat's prohibition does not apply. Nagoa Beach, the island's largest beach, is accessible by motorcycle taxi from town. Evenings on Diu are quiet: no loud nightlife, just a few seaside bars.
