visits.text: Not many travelers stop at Eluru—a mistake. The Kolleru Bird Sanctuary covers 673 square kilometers between the Krishna and Godavari deltas and constitutes one of India's largest freshwater lakes. The site has been designated a Ramsar wetland since 2002. Between October and March, migratory birds arrive from Siberia: painted storks, glossy ibises, ducks, geese, and swans. Access on foot from the shores; boat available at Atapaka.

activities.text: You board a boat at sunrise on Kolleru: herons and cormorants take off as you approach, and water lilies are still closing their flowers in the calm water. The ride lasts about an hour from the fishing village of Atapaka. Rate negotiated directly with local fishermen.

visits.text: Arrival at Ernakulam Junction after the night on the train. Take the local ferry (15 min) to Fort Kochi - it is the best way to arrive, with the silhouette of the Chinese fishing nets taking shape from the boat. These huge cantilevered nets, called “Cheena Vala” in Malayalam, are said to have been introduced by Chinese traders in the 14th century, possibly by the fleet of the explorer Zheng He.

Step through the door of St. Francis Church, the oldest European church in India. Built in wood by Portuguese Franciscans in 1503, then rebuilt in stone in 1516, it housed Vasco da Gama's burial after his death in Kochi in 1524 - his remains were later repatriated to Lisbon in 1539. Portuguese tombstones are on the north wall, Dutch ones on the south. The church is open from 9am to 5pm (except Sunday morning).

Continue to Mattancherry for the Dutch Palace, built by the Portuguese around 1555 then renovated by the Dutch in 1663. Don't be fooled by the modest exterior: inside, the 17th-century murals illustrating the Ramayana are among Kerala's finest. Right next door, Jew Town and the Paradesi Synagogue (1568) - one of the Commonwealth's oldest active synagogues - are worth the detour for their hand-painted floor tiles imported from China.

activities.text: Fort Kochi is best explored on foot - the lanes are lined with Portuguese, Dutch and British colonial houses, interspersed with contemporary art galleries and cafes in former spice warehouses. If the Kochi Biennale (every 2 years, December to March) is on, art installations take over historic buildings - Aspinwall House, the old harbor warehouse, is the main site.

In the evening, attend a Kathakali performance (Kerala's dance-theater with spectacular makeup) at one of Fort Kochi's cultural centers - shows generally start around 6:30pm with a makeup demonstration 1 hour before. Otherwise, return to the Chinese nets at sunset: fishermen operate the wooden counterweights, and the low light on the nets creates Kerala's most photographed cliché.

places.name: Goa

visits.text: Old Goa, 10 km from Panaji, is the historic heart of Portuguese colonisation — the 'Rome of the East' in the 16th century. The Basilica of Bom Jesus (1605), UNESCO-listed, houses the body of Saint Francis Xavier in a silver coffin. The Jesuit missionary died in 1552, but his body is said to be 'incorrupt' — it's publicly displayed every ten years (last time in 2024). The Baroque interior is restrained compared to the façades, but the gilded altarpiece is striking.

Just across the way, the Sé Cathedral is the largest church in Asia — 76 metres long, built between 1562 and 1640. It has only one tower (the second collapsed in 1776 and was never rebuilt). Inside, the Chapel of the Blessed Sacrament is covered in gilding. Allow 30 minutes for both churches together.

In the afternoon, head south to the beaches — Palolem is a crescent-shaped cove fringed with coconut palms, bookended by rocky headlands at each end. The water is calm, ideal for swimming. It's Goa's most photogenic beach, but also the busiest in peak season. If you're after more peace and quiet, continue to Agonda, 5 km further north — same scenery, fewer people.

Panaji (Panjim), Goa's capital, has a hidden Latin Quarter: Fontainhas. This tangle of narrow streets lined with houses painted yellow, blue and ochre is the last vestige of the old Portuguese district. The wrought-iron balconies, azulejos (glazed earthenware tiles) and corner chapels transport you to Lisbon. Allow an hour to wander with camera in hand.

Chapora Fort, reached on an excursion from Panaji and made famous by Indian cinema, offers a 360° panorama of the coast - Vagator's beaches below and the mouth of the Chapora River. Its red laterite walls stand out against the sky. Only ruins remain (the fort dates from 1717), but the view, rather than the architecture, is what makes this place special. Climb up in the late afternoon for the light.

activities.text: Taste Goan cuisine — a unique blend of Indian and Portuguese influences. Vindaloo (pork marinated in vinegar and spices) and xacuti (chicken with coconut and spices) are the signature dishes. Pair them with feni, the local spirit distilled from cashew nuts or coconut palm sap.
Sunset on the beach — it's a ritual in Goa. Beach shacks serve grilled fish as you sit with your feet in the sand and the sun plunges into the Arabian Sea. A simple, perfect moment.

If you're here on a Friday, don't miss the Mapusa Market — the most authentic in Goa. Spices, chouriço sausages, tropical fruits, dried fish and local handicrafts. It's loud, colourful and thoroughly local.

In the evening, prepare for the Goa → Kochi leg: the Netravati Express (16345) departs Madgaon around 10:40 PM and arrives at Ernakulam Junction the next day around 12:20 PM — roughly 14 hours overnight. This is the famous Konkan Railway, one of the most beautiful train lines in the world: the track hugs the west coast, crossing 2,000 bridges and 92 tunnels between mountains and sea. Book an AC2 sleeper for a comfortable night. The Mangala Lakshadweep Express is another daily option. Reserve 4–5 days ahead on IRCTC.

visits.text: Locals still call it 'Golla Konda'—the shepherd's hill. Golconda Fort was transformed by the Qutb Shahis into an impregnable citadel with 10 km of ramparts and 87 bastions. The trick: clap your hands beneath the dome of Fateh Darwaza—the sound travels up to the summit nearly a kilometer away. The Koh-i-Noor passed through here before landing in London.

Seventy domed tombs rise from the gardens of Ibrahim Bagh, some gilded for sultans, others more austere for nobles. The Qutb Shahi Tombs were restored between 2013 and 2019 by the Aga Khan Trust. Entry requires effort: arrive on a weekday to appreciate the silence between the structures.

activities.text: Stay for the evening sound and light show at Golconda Fort: Amitabh Bachchan's voice narrates the 1687 siege by Aurangzeb. The performance lasts about 45 minutes. Book your ticket early—numbered seats sell out fast on weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: Deccan: Bahmani Sultans and Kakatiya Temples in 12 Days

visits.text: Once a Kalinga trading port mentioned by Ptolemy under the name Paloura, Gopalpur has retained the melancholy of a forgotten town. Dilapidated colonial villas line quiet lanes, and the golden beach, bordered by casuarinas, is uncrowded. Known to Europeans since the colonial era, this resort served as a military port during World War I.

The white lighthouse, built in 1965, stands at the far end of the beach. Open to visitors in the afternoon (variable hours), it offers 360-degree views over the Bay of Bengal and Chilika Lagoon in the distance. Modest height but unobstructed views. Nominal entry fee.

activities.text: Take your meals at the fishermen's shacks lining the beach: crabs, shrimp, and grilled fish caught that same morning. The cooking is simple and good. The Nolias, local fishermen, haul their nets by hand on the beach at dawn. Don't swim—currents are dangerous year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: From Coast to Jungle: Bhubaneswar to Bhopal in 16 Days

visits.text: Hampi has been a UNESCO site since 1986—the ruins of the former Vijayanagara Empire capital (14th-16th centuries) sprawl across 26 km² among enormous ochre granite boulders. Begin with Virupaksha Temple, the only one still active, dedicated to Shiva. Its 50-meter gopuram tower dominates the main bazaar. Inside, in a dark chamber, you'll witness an astonishing phenomenon: the inverted image of the gopuram projects naturally onto the wall through a camera obscura effect. Arrive early morning to beat the heat—it can be crushing after 11am.

Continue to Vittala Temple, 2.5 km northeast. This is Hampi's jewel: its stone chariot, drawn by carved elephants, appears on 50-rupee notes. The 56 musical pillars in the main hall produce different notes when struck—a 16th-century engineering feat. Take a tuk-tuk or rent a bicycle to connect the two temples; walking in full sun is exhausting.

activities.text: Late in the day, climb Matanga Hill for sunset. The ascent takes about 20 minutes via a rocky trail—wear good shoes and bring water. From the summit, the 360° view over the ruins, rice paddies, Tungabhadra River, and granite boulders is one of Karnataka's most beautiful. Descend before dark—the path isn't lit.

To explore the ruins further afield, rent a bicycle for the day and tour the royal enclosure: the Lotus Mahal (a pavilion in Indo-Islamic style), the elephant stables (eleven aligned domes), and the Queen's Bath. Allow 2 to 3 hours to cover this area by bike at a leisurely pace.

days_plan.itin_title: South India Circuit: Temples, Backwaters & Wellness

visits.text: Haridwar is only 25 km from Rishikesh but the vibe is totally different—here, no hippies or trendy cafés. It's one of Hinduism's seven holiest cities, where the Ganges officially enters the plains. The city's heart is Har Ki Pauri, the most sacred ghat, where a footprint of Vishnu is said to be carved in stone. This is where millions of pilgrims come for ritual bathing. Every 12 years, Haridwar hosts the Kumbh Mela, the world's largest human gathering—over 100 million people in 2021.

Take the cable car (or walk up, 45 min) to Mansa Devi Temple, perched on a Shivalik ridge 300 meters above the city. The panoramic view of Haridwar, the Ganges, and the Gangetic plains stretching to the horizon is spectacular. The temple is dedicated to the goddess Mansa, who grants wishes—you'll see red threads tied by devotees.

On the opposite hill, Chandi Devi Temple (also accessible by cable car) is said to date from the 8th century and to have been founded by the philosopher Adi Shankaracharya. The walk up (3 km) passes through a forest with valley views—pleasant in the morning when it's cool.

activities.text: Attend Ganga Aarti at Har Ki Pauri at sunset - it's older and more 'authentic' than Rishikesh's, less packaged for tourists. Thousands of devotees crowd the ghats, temple bells ring, incense smoke mingles with river mist. Place a diya (floating lamp) on the Ganges and watch it drift in the current.

Wander through Bara Bazaar, Haridwar's main market. You'll find vessels for carrying Ganges water home (a sacred souvenir for Hindus), rudraksha (prayer beads), deity statues, and traditional sweets. The atmosphere is frenetic and colorful.

Sample Haridwar's strict vegetarian cuisine - the entire city is vegetarian (alcohol and meat are banned). Dhabas (eateries) around Har Ki Pauri serve complete thalis, kachori, and thick lassi. Haridwar's chole bhature is famous across North India.

visits.text: Built in 1591 to mark the end of a devastating epidemic, Charminar was the first monument erected by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah in his new capital of Hyderabad. The structure soars to 56 meters, flanked by four minarets framing a still-bustling crossroads. Climb to the second level for views over the bazaar: entry is free before 5 p.m., after which access becomes complicated.

Chowmahalla Palace deserves a full hour: this former seat of the Nizams was constructed in the 18th century, blending Mughal domes with Persian stuccowork. The Durbar Hall with its crystal chandelier leaves visitors speechless. Closed on Fridays; plan for ₹100 (foreign visitors: ₹400).

The call to prayer echoes through Mecca Masjid, one of the Deccan's largest mosques, whose construction spanned several decades under the Qutb Shahis and later the Mughals. The monolithic columns of the portico each weigh several tons. Enter early in the morning, before the Friday rush.

Touristy, perhaps, but Salar Jung Museum harbors improbable treasures: a 19th-century English automaton, Mughal miniatures, and a collection of jade daggers. The sprawling building on the Musi riverbank easily requires two hours. Arrive at opening to avoid school groups.

activities.text: Dive into the lanes of Laad Bazaar, famous for its lacquered bangles that have encircled the base of Charminar for centuries. The colors range from emerald to crimson; bargaining is expected, wandering is encouraged. Bring cash—small vendors don't take cards.

If you walk from Charminar at sunset, the golden light on the minarets creates an image photographs never quite capture. The stroll toward Purani Haveli takes 20 minutes. Wear closed shoes—the lanes are unevenly paved.

days_plan.itin_title: Deccan: Bahmani Sultans and Kakatiya Temples in 12 Days

visits.text: See the Hawa Mahal (Palace of Winds) early in the morning when the sun strikes the facade—that's the best time. This 15-meter pink sandstone wall, built in 1799 by Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh, contains 953 honeycomb windows. Architect Lal Chand Ustad designed it in the shape of Krishna's crown. The jharokhas allowed royal women to observe street processions without being seen. Surprising detail: the building has no foundation. Entry is from the rear, not the facade—look carefully.

Jaipur has been a trading city since its founding in 1727 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II—one of India's first grid-plan cities. Johari Bazaar for gemstones, Tripolia Bazaar for textiles and lac bangles, Bapu Bazaar for souvenirs. Stop for roadside chai—often offered by shopkeepers hoping you'll linger.

The City Palace of Jaipur is still partially inhabited by the royal family. The Mubarak Mahal (Palace of Welcome), built in the late 19th century, houses a royal textile museum. Don't miss the two giant silver urns in the Diwan-i-Khas—standing 1.60 m tall, they're the world's largest solid silver objects (Guinness record). They carried Ganges water on royal trips to England.

Right next to the City Palace, Jantar Mantar is an astronomical observatory built in 1734 by Sawai Jai Singh II. Its 19 monumental stone instruments have been UNESCO-listed since 2010. The most imposing: the Samrat Yantra, the world's largest sundial—27 meters tall, accurate to within 2 seconds. Hire a guide on-site, or the instruments remain incomprehensible.

If you have energy late in the day, head to Galtaji (Monkey Temple) 10 km east. Nestled in a rocky gorge, this 18th-century temple complex is overrun by macaques. Natural pools fed by springs are sacred. The main temple dedicated to Hanuman is decorated with murals. Guard your belongings from the monkeys—they're quick and opportunistic.

Start with Nahargarh Fort at dawn—the view over Jaipur from the ramparts is the city's finest. Built in 1734 by Sawai Jai Singh II then expanded in 1868, the fort dominates the Aravalli ridge. Inside lies Madhavendra Bhawan, with its symmetrical suites built for the maharaja's nine queens. If you're athletic, cycle up from the city—the road is steep but spectacular.

Descending, stop at Jal Mahal (Water Palace) for the photo. This 18th-century palace seems to float in the middle of Man Sagar Lake—in reality, four of its five floors are submerged. You can't enter, but the view from the shore, especially with the Aravalli backdrop, is one of Rajasthan's classic postcards.

The royal cenotaphs of Gaitore, nestled in a valley between Nahargarh and the city, are often ignored by tourists. These are the tombs of Jaipur's maharajas—the most elaborate, in carved white marble, are those of Sawai Jai Singh II and Sawai Pratap Singh. The place is peaceful and photogenic, especially in the morning.

Amber Fort is the most spectacular monument in the Jaipur region. Built from 1592 by Raja Man Singh I on a hill overlooking Lake Maota, it blends Rajput and Mughal architecture. The Sheesh Mahal (Mirror Palace) inside is dazzling—thousands of convex mirror fragments line walls and ceilings. The Diwan-i-Aam courtyard and the Ganesh Pol (with its colored tile mosaic) are unmissable. The fort is one of six Rajasthani forts UNESCO-listed in 2013. Allow at least 2 hours.

Just below Amber Fort, don't miss Panna Meena ka Kund—a 16th-century geometric stepwell whose zigzagging staircases create a hypnotic pattern. Highly photogenic, and far less crowded than Abhaneri's Chand Baori.

If Indian textiles interest you, head to the Anokhi Museum in Amber, housed in a restored haveli. It traces the history of block printing (hand-stamping on fabric), an ancestral Rajasthani technique. Artisan demonstrations are often offered.

activities.text: Take a guided bicycle tour of Jaipur at dawn, before the heat and traffic. Several operators offer 2–3-hour tours through the old city, with stops at the flower and vegetable markets, and breakfast in a local home.
Late in the day, settle on the ramparts of Amber for sunset. The golden light on the Aravalli hills and Lake Maota below creates a sumptuous scene. Bring water—there are no vendors at the top.

visits.text: Jaisalmer Fort is one of the last still-inhabited fortresses, with around 3,000 people living within its golden sandstone walls. Founded in 1156 by Rawal Jaisal, it rises 76 metres above the Thar Desert on Trikuta Hill. Its golden stone earned it the nickname “Sonar Quila” (Golden Fort) - at sunset, the ramparts seem to melt into the sand. Inside, visit the 12th-century Jain temples, including Chandraprabhu Temple, whose sculptures are astonishingly delicate - every centimetre of stone is carved.

Head down to the lower town to explore the havelis — grand old mansions of fabulously wealthy merchants, carved from the same golden sandstone as the fort. Start with Patwon Ki Haveli, the largest — five adjoining buildings constructed between 1805 and 1862 by a family that traded in brocade and opium. Every balcony, every window is a lacework of stone. Then move on to Nathmal Ki Haveli, built by two brothers who each worked on one side — spot the subtle differences between the two halves; it's a fun game.

Gadisar Lake, a 10-minute walk from the fort, is an artificial reservoir dug in 1367 by Maharawal Gadsi Singh. The entrance is through a carved gateway. Early in the morning, the fort's reflection in the still water is stunning. You can rent a pedal boat or simply sit on the ghats.

activities.text: Take an excursion into the Thar Desert to the Sam Sand Dunes, 42 km from Jaisalmer. Operators offer late-afternoon outings to catch the sunset over the dunes — by dromedary or by jeep. The sight of golden dunes bathed in low-angle light is breathtaking. If you spend the night in a tent, the Thar's starry sky, free from light pollution, is one of the most beautiful in India. You can return the same evening if you'd rather sleep in town.

visits.text: A detour worth taking: Sri Ketaki Sangameswara Swamy Temple in the village of Jharasangam is the only known exception to the Hindu rule forbidding ketaki flowers as offerings to Shiva. According to local legend, King Kupendra was cured of a skin disease after bathing in the temple's spring. Open from 5:30 a.m. to 9 p.m.; no accommodation on-site, continue to Bidar.

places.name: Jodhpur

visits.text: Mehrangarh dominates Jodhpur from a 125-meter rocky spur—it's one of India's most massive forts. Built from 1459 by Rao Jodha, it houses a remarkable museum with an excellent audio guide available in French. The collections of palanquins, armor and royal cradles are exceptional. Pass through Loha Pol gate—you'll see the handprints of queens who committed sati (immolation on their husband's funeral pyre). Allow 2 to 3 hours for the complete visit.

From Mehrangarh's ramparts, you'll understand why Jodhpur is the 'Blue City'—the indigo blue of the Brahmin quarter's houses stretches endlessly below. Descend into the lanes to lose yourself in this labyrinth of bright blue facades, carved doors and nonchalant cows. The best viewpoints are from the guesthouse terraces in the Navchokiya quarter.

Jaswant Thada, a 5-minute walk from Mehrangarh, is a white marble cenotaph built in 1899 in memory of Maharaja Jaswant Singh II. The marble is so thin it's translucent in sunlight. The garden and small artificial lake surrounding it make this a haven of peace after the fort's intensity.

Below the Clock Tower, Sardar Market is Jodhpur's beating heart—spices (Rajasthani red chili, turmeric), lac bangles, tie-dye textiles and miniatures. If you're seeking the city's best lassi, follow the locals—the most popular stalls are always the most crowded.

Push on to Toorji Ka Jhalra, an 18th-century stepwell recently restored, hidden among the old city houses. Less monumental than Bundi's, but the turquoise water and geometric stairs make it an unexpected photo spot.

Mandore Gardens, 9 km north of Jodhpur, shelter the cenotaphs of the Marwar rulers in a shaded park. The dewals (funerary temples) in red sandstone are carved with Hindu figures. The place is frequented by local families in the morning—a good glimpse of daily life away from tourist circuits. Watch for langurs, which are numerous and bold.

Rao Jodha Desert Rock Park, at the foot of Mehrangarh, is a 72-hectare ecological reserve created to restore desert vegetation. Marked trails traverse a landscape of volcanic rocks and endemic plants—euphorbias, commiphoras, acacias. If you enjoy walking, it's the perfect complement to the fort visit, with different views of the ramparts.

Umaid Bhawan Palace, part luxury hotel and part royal family residence, is worth at least a look from the outside. Built between 1929 and 1943, it's one of the last great palaces constructed in India—347 rooms, in sandstone and marble. The interior museum displays Art Deco collections and palace models.

activities.text: Operators offer zipline rides above Mehrangarh's ramparts and lakes—6 lines spanning 1.2 km with views looking down over the blue city and fort. Thrills guaranteed. Book the day before.

Set out on an excursion to the Bishnoi villages, 30 km from Jodhpur. The Bishnoi are a community known for protecting nature since the 15th century—they live in harmony with local wildlife (antelopes, gazelles, demoiselle cranes). Several operators offer half-day tours that also include visits to potters and weavers.

visits.text: Uparkot Fort is said to have been founded in 319 BCE by Chandragupta's Mauryan Empire—and archaeologists don't really contradict the date. The ramparts can reach 20 meters high in places. Sixteen sieges failed to take it; one reportedly lasted twelve years according to local tradition. Inside: two wells cut into living rock, a Buddhist cave complex, and an Ottoman cannon brought from Diu.

From Uparkot's ramparts, Girnar Hills dominate the eastern horizon—this volcanic massif shelters Jain and Hindu temples as well as the famous engraved edicts of Ashoka, among the oldest texts in Brahmi script. Girnar has a ropeway for travelers who prefer not to climb the steps.

Head up to Mahabat Maqbara, a 19th-century mausoleum dedicated to Bahaduddinbhai Hasainbhai, Nawab of Junagadh. Its facade fuses neo-Gothic pillars, Mughal balconies, and silver arabesques—a monument of unabashed architectural eccentricity. It can be viewed freely from the street.

activities.text: If your fitness allows, the roughly 10,000 steps leading to Girnar's summit temples are traditionally climbed at night to arrive at dawn. Pilgrims depart after midnight. For a more accessible version, the ropeway (Girnar Ropeway) serves the intermediate temples in minutes.

visits.text: Covering 235 km², Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary stretches across the Godavari estuary about twenty kilometers from Kakinada. It is home to more than 120 bird species, saltwater crocodiles, and the rare fishing cat. Open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; closed on Tuesdays. Admission is inexpensive.

River and sea merge into a blurred horizon at the Godavari mouth, visible from Coringa sanctuary. This estuary landscape—brown river waters meeting the blue-gray Bay of Bengal—looks like nothing else on the east coast. Best light late afternoon.

If weather permits, rent a boat at Kakinada port to reach Hope Island, an hour's crossing across the bay. This barrier island is a nesting site for olive ridley turtles and a bird refuge. No lodging on site; the return trip is in the afternoon. Check that the boat service is running before leaving—it's sometimes suspended.

Uppada Beach doesn't look like much from the road, but the traditional fishing nets stretched between wooden poles make it one of the delta coast's characteristic sights. Fishermen head out again before dawn; by 7 a.m., the nets have already been retrieved. The beach remains little visited by tourists.

activities.text: You walk along the 600-meter wooden boardwalk that snakes through the mangrove canopy: the roots of Rhizophora plunge downward, framing the path, and kingfishers fly through the green shade. The boardwalk leads to a viewpoint over the estuary. Wear sturdy shoes; the wood can be slippery.

visits.text: Gulbarga Fort sees fewer visitors than Bidar, which is its main virtue. Originally built by a Kakatiya feudatory, it was fortified by the Bahmani in a half-Persian, half-Indian style. Inside, Jama Masjid oddly resembles Córdoba's Great Mosque: dozens of low domes on columns, no dominant minaret. Free entry.

Khwaja Bande Nawaz lived here for 22 years until the age of 105, spreading Sufism across the Deccan at Sultan Firuz's invitation. His dargah draws pilgrims from three states. The architecture blends Bahmani arches with Turco-Iranian paintings. Remove shoes at the entrance and cover your head.

activities.text: Detour to Haft Gumbaz, seven Bahmani dynastic tombs outside town. The complex is semi-abandoned, giving it an atmosphere over-restored sites have lost. Expect a 30-minute walk through a grassy field. No admission fee.

visits.text: Enjoy Varkala in the morning - walk down the steps to Papanasam Beach (the “beach that washes away sins”) for a morning swim. The water is warm all year. Freshwater springs emerge from the cliff directly onto the beach - a rare phenomenon. Then climb back up the cliff steps, stopping at the small cafés perched above.

Take a ferry from Kanyakumari to reach Vivekananda Rock, 500 meters offshore. It was on this rock that the Hindu monk Swami Vivekananda meditated in 1892 before delivering his famous speech at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago. The memorial, built in 1970, blends architectural styles from across India. Right next to it, the statue of Thiruvalluvar—a 2nd-century Tamil poet—rises 40 meters above the ocean. Ferries depart every 30 minutes and the crossing takes 10 minutes. Avoid weekends and public holidays—the wait in line can be 2 hours.

activities.text: Kanyakumari is the southernmost point of India, where the Indian Ocean, Arabian Sea, and Bay of Bengal meet. Sunset from the Sunset View Point is the highlight: you'll see the sun plunge into the sea at the exact spot where three bodies of water converge. Arrive 30 minutes early to secure a good spot—all of Kanyakumari gathers here.

End your circuit with a stroll along the Kanyakumari seafront. The seashell stands, chai stalls, and sea breeze offer a peaceful conclusion to your journey. The nearest airport is Trivandrum (Thiruvananthapuram), 90 km to the north—allow 2 hours' drive to reach it.

days_plan.itin_title: Tamil Nadu and Kerala Road Trip: Temples and Backwaters

visits.text: The Chettinad region, 90 km south of Trichy, is one of Tamil Nadu's best-kept secrets. In the 75 villages around Karaikudi, more than 10,000 palatial mansions were built by the Nattukottai Chettiars, a merchant community that made fortunes in maritime trade with Southeast Asia during the 19th and 20th centuries. The mansions blend Italian marble columns, Burmese teak, European stained glass, and handmade Athangudi tiles—a combination unique in the world. Many are closed, but a few like the VVR Palace welcome visitors for a modest fee.

Kanadukathan Palace, which you can visit on a round trip from Karaikudi, is the most spectacular of the Chettinad mansions. Built in 1912 by Dr Annamalai Chettiyar (founder of Indian Bank and Annamalai University), it has around a hundred rooms decorated with Spanish marble columns and crystal chandeliers. A visit requires prior permission—ask your accommodation to arrange this. Some of these mansions have been converted into heritage hotels—spending the night in one is an experience in itself.

activities.text: Chettinad cuisine is renowned throughout India for its powerful spices—black pepper, star anise, fennel, and dried chili. If your accommodation offers it, don't miss a traditional meal served on a banana leaf. The Chettinad Chicken you may know from restaurants will be on a completely different level here—warning, it's seriously spicy.

Explore the villages on foot—every street corner reveals a new palace, a colorful temple, or a sacred tank. The temples of Ayyanar, the village guardian, with their giant terracotta equestrian statues, are typical of this region. Drive slowly between hamlets and let yourself be surprised by the scale of these mansions in the middle of the Tamil countryside.

visits.text: 182 meters: the Statue of Unity looms before the car even reaches Kevadia. Inaugurated on October 31, 2018, the world's tallest statue is dedicated to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, independent India's first Deputy Prime Minister, who unified over 565 princely states. The height of 182 meters corresponds exactly to the number of seats in the Gujarat Legislative Assembly. The observation gallery, at 135 meters, accommodates up to 200 visitors at a time overlooking the Narmada.

activities.text: Ascend to the observation gallery at 135 meters to look out over the Narmada River and Sardar Sarovar Dam framed by the Satpura and Vindhyachal hills. The complex also includes the Valley of Flowers, a museum, and a river cruise. Book tickets online at soutickets.in—queues can be long on weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: Gujarat: Grand Tour of UNESCO Sites in 15 Days

visits.text: Khajuraho is about 4 hours by road from Orchha. UNESCO-listed since 1986, it's one of India's most extraordinary sites. Of the 85 temples built by the Chandela dynasty between 950 and 1050 AD, 25 have survived—and their sculptures are stunningly refined. Start with the Western Group, the most spectacular. Kandariya Mahadeva temple is the largest and most elaborate: its walls are covered with nearly 900 sculptures depicting deities, celestial nymphs (apsaras), and the famous entwined couples (mithuna). Contrary to popular belief, erotic scenes represent only about 10% of the sculptures—the rest shows daily life, war, music, and dance.

Lakshmana temple, dedicated to Vishnu, is one of the best preserved. Built under King Yashovarman around 950, it rests on a high platform adorned with a continuous frieze of sculptures—elephants, horses, and scenes of battle and court life. Take time to walk all the way around the temple to appreciate the progression of the sculptures, from the earthly world at the base toward the divine at the top.

Don't neglect the Eastern Group, 20 minutes' walk away. The Jain temples of Parsvanath and Adinath are less famous but equally finely carved, with floral motifs and apsaras of remarkable grace. The contrast between Hindu and Jain temples side by side testifies to the Chandela era's religious tolerance.

activities.text: Attend the sound and light show within the Western Group enclosure - it recounts Chandela history and temple construction. The show lasts about 50 minutes and takes place after sunset. The dramatic nighttime lighting of the temples alone is worth the trip.
Explore Khajuraho's small Archaeological Museum, which displays sculptures recovered from destroyed temple sites. Some pieces match the quality of those still in place on the temples.

Walk through Khajuraho village late afternoon - it remains surprisingly rural and quiet despite tourism. Local markets sell stone and wood carvings that imitate (with varying success) the temple style.

visits.text: Khammam is a transit stop on NH163, midway between Bhadrachalam and Mancherial. Khammam Fort, built on a rock overlooking the town, dates from the Kakatiya period. A brief stop for dinner and an overnight stay—the town has good accommodation options.

days_plan.itin_title: From Coast to Jungle: Bhubaneswar to Bhopal in 16 Days

visits.text: Two hills that look unremarkable from the road, yet 33 Jain caves were carved into them in the 2nd century BCE—18 on Udayagiri and 15 on Khandagiri. Commissioned by King Kharavela of the Mahameghavahana dynasty, these shelters housed monks during monsoon retreats. The Rani Gumpha cave has two stories and is decorated with scenes of royal processions. Allow 1.5 hours for both hills. Closed-toe shoes are essential.

You climb Udayagiri to reach Hathi Gumpha, where Kharavela's inscription carved in Prakrit details his conquests—one of ancient India's most important epigraphic texts. At the top of Khandagiri, an 18th-century Jain temple offers 360-degree views over Bhubaneswar. Sunrise recommended.

activities.text: The city of Bhubaneswar sprawls beneath your feet from the summit of Khandagiri: minarets, temple domes, green patches of parks. This morning panorama is free and largely ignored by organized tours. Bring water; the climb is short but exposed.

days_plan.itin_title: From Coast to Jungle: Bhubaneswar to Bhopal in 16 Days

places.name: Kochi

visits.text: You land at Cochin International Airport in Nedumbassery, roughly 40 km from Fort Kochi. Plan on a solid hour's drive to reach the historic quarter—the route cuts through paddy fields and coconut-lined canals that set the tone for the entire journey. Check into your accommodation and take time to acclimatize to Kerala's humid warmth.

Late afternoon, head to Fort Kochi Beach promenade to witness the Chinese fishing nets—massive structures of teak and bamboo mounted on granite counterweights, in use since the 14th century and introduced, according to tradition, by merchants from Kublai Khan's court. The spectacle peaks at sunset, when fishermen work the nets by sheer muscle power. If hunger strikes, vendors right beside the nets will grill the fresh fish you pick from their catch.

Start at St. Francis Church, built of timber in 1503 by Portuguese Franciscan friars—it's the oldest European church in India. The current stone building dates to 1516. Vasco da Gama was buried here in 1524 during his third voyage to India; his remains weren't repatriated to Lisbon until 14 years later, but you'll still see his tombstone inside. The church passed from Portuguese hands to the Dutch in 1663, then to the British in 1795—each occupant left its mark. Free entry, open 9am–5pm except during Sunday services.

A few minutes' walk brings you to Santa Cruz Cathedral Basilica, originally erected by the Portuguese in 1505 and rebuilt in its present neo-Gothic form in 1902. The interior will surprise you—pastel ceiling frescoes and a richly carved altar offer a burst of color that contrasts sharply with the whitewashed exterior. Stained-glass windows filter soft light into the nave, lending it a contemplative atmosphere even at midday.

Catch an auto-rickshaw or ferry to Mattancherry to visit Paradesi Synagogue, built in 1568 by Sephardic Jews who fled Spain and Portugal. The floor is paved with hundreds of hand-painted porcelain tiles imported from Canton in the 18th century—each one unique. 19th-century Belgian crystal chandeliers sparkle above a brass pulpit. The synagogue also preserves copper plates engraved in ancient Malayalam 1,600 years ago, detailing privileges granted to the Jewish community by the Cochin raja. Note: closed on Fridays, Saturdays, and Jewish holidays. Enter barefoot.

Exiting the synagogue, lose yourself in the alleys of Jew Town and Mattancherry spice market. The air is thick with cardamom, pepper, turmeric, and cloves—the same spices that drew Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs, and Europeans to this coast for millennia. Antique shops overflow with colonial furniture, vintage porcelain, and old coins. Bargain, but keep in mind that prices here are already more reasonable than Delhi or Mumbai.

The drive from Varkala to Kochi (184 km, 3.5 hours) takes you back north. If you leave early, you'll have time to visit Mattancherry Palace (also called the Dutch Palace), built by the Portuguese in 1555 as a gift to the Cochin raja, then renovated by the Dutch in 1663—hence its nickname. Don't miss the 17th-century murals illustrating scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata—they rank among Kerala's finest wall paintings. The palace also houses royal portraits, palanquins, and ceremonial garments.

If your flight is in the evening, use the remaining time to explore Jew Town's antique shops—vintage ceramics, textiles, and brass objects. Or enjoy one last Keralan meal at a Fort Kochi restaurant: a full thali with rice boat (rice shaped like a boat), fried fish, mango pickle, and payasam for dessert. Cochin International Airport is about 1 hour 15 minutes from Fort Kochi—allow a comfortable margin.

activities.text: Wander through Fort Kochi's lanes as dusk falls. Portuguese, Dutch, and British colonial facades succeed one another within a few hundred meters—an architectural palimpsest found nowhere else in India. You'll stumble upon contemporary art galleries installed in former spice warehouses, cafés tucked into Dutch houses, and street art murals. The atmosphere is serene, a world apart from the chaos of India's megacities.

In the evening, attend a Kathakali dance performance. This four-century-old theatrical form from Kerala blends dance, mime, and music. Artists spend over an hour applying makeup—green faces for heroes, red for villains—using natural pigments applied in layers. Arrive 30 minutes before the show to watch the makeup application, often open to the public. Count on around 1.5 hours for the full experience.

Before leaving Kerala, if time allows, swing by Broadway Market in Ernakulam (the mainland part of Kochi). This covered market, far less touristy than Mattancherry, is where locals buy their spices, fabrics, and kitchen utensils. You'll find black pepper, green cardamom, and turmeric powder at unbeatable prices—perfect for useful souvenirs.

visits.text: Leave Alleppey southward for Kollam (70 km, 2 hours), one of the world's oldest trading ports. Marco Polo described it in the 13th century under the name "Coilum," and Ibn Battuta in the 14th century counted it among the five greatest ports he'd seen in 24 years of travel. Phoenicians, Romans, Chinese, and Arabs traded spices, silk, and porcelain here for millennia. Today, the town is the global cashew capital—you'll catch the roasting aroma in certain neighborhoods.

Visit Ashtamudi Lake, Kerala's second-largest body of water, a Ramsar-designated wetland. Its name means "eight arms" in Malayalam, referring to the eight channels branching through the mangroves. It's the southern gateway to the backwaters, far quieter than Alleppey. If you haven't had your fill of canals, a short cruise on Ashtamudi will offer wilder scenery, with coconut palms leaning over the water and sleepy fishing villages.

Make a detour to Munroe Island (Munroethuruthu), an archipelago of eight small islands where the Ashtamudi meets the Kallada River; allow half a day for the round trip from Kollam. You get there by road, then explore the canals by boat. Life has remained almost unchanged - copra drying, toddy (palm wine) making, prawn fishing in the canals. Allow 2 to 3 hours for a boat trip with a local guide.

activities.text: Late in the day, climb Thangassery Lighthouse, a relic of Portuguese and then Dutch presence on this coast. From the top, the view sweeps across the Arabian Sea and the red roofs of the old colonial quarter. Thangassery was the first European trading post established in Kollam in 1502. Catch the sunset from the adjacent beach.

visits.text: Ten kilometers before you arrive, the silhouette of Konark Sun Temple already cuts across the sky. Built around 1250 by Narasimhadeva I of the Ganga dynasty, this monumental stone chariot represents the vehicle of the god Surya: 24 sculpted wheels, seven rearing horses. UNESCO-listed since 1984. The main tower collapsed in the 16th century; what remains is already dizzying. Hire an accredited guide at the entrance; the erotic and astronomical details need explaining.

At the Konark Archaeological Museum, just opposite the temple, you'll find sculptures recovered during excavations: horsemen, dancers, nagarajas. Less crowded than the temple, this is often where the finest pieces reside. Closed Fridays. Allow 40 minutes.

activities.text: Chandrabhaga Beach, 3 km from the temple, hosts the Magha Saptami festival each February when thousands of pilgrims come to bathe at sunrise. Outside the festival, it's an uncrowded, clean beach with colorful fishing nets. Swimming not recommended—strong currents. Excellent for photographing dawn.

visits.text: Leave Mumbai via the Mumbai-Pune Expressway (115 km, 2.5 hours) heading to Lonavala, a hill station perched in the Western Ghats. The road snakes through tunnels and verdant valleys—during monsoon, waterfalls gush everywhere, but in the dry season the landscape is more arid.

Your first stop: Karla Caves, which house India's largest rock-cut Buddhist chaitya (prayer hall). Built between the 2nd century BC and 2nd century AD, this hall measures 45 meters long and 14 meters high—an underground cathedral carved from basalt. What strikes you first are the teak wood ribs on the ceiling: most are original, still in place after more than 2,000 years. The 37 octagonal pillars are topped with sculptures of couples riding elephants—a liveliness and naturalism that makes you forget their age. Count on 350 steps to climb from the base of the hill.

Eight kilometers from Karla, Bhaja Caves are a complex of 22 Buddhist caves from the 2nd century BC, contemporary with Karla but far less crowded. You'll find stupas, remarkable narrative sculptures, and an atmosphere of contemplative solitude that Karla has lost to tourism. Access requires about 200 steps on a rocky path—the views across the valley from the top are worth the effort.

activities.text: At the end of the day, enjoy Lonavala—the town itself is nothing exceptional, but the fresh air of the Ghats and the views from viewpoints such as Tiger's Leap, reached by car from Lonavala, or Rajmachi Point are welcome after the heat of Mumbai. Try chikki, the local specialty—a crunchy sweet made with jaggery (unrefined cane sugar) and peanuts, sold throughout town.

visits.text: The Meenakshi Amman Temple is arguably the most spectacular temple in all of South India — and the one monument that justifies the detour to Madurai on its own. Its 14 gopurams (gateway towers) soar up to 52 metres high and are covered in thousands of brightly painted sculptures — gods, goddesses, demons, mythical creatures. The current temple dates from the 17th century under the Nayak dynasty, but a sanctuary has stood here for at least 2,000 years. Inside, 33,000 sculptures adorn the corridors. The sacred Golden Lotus Tank (Potramarai Kulam) sits at the heart of the complex. Visit early in the morning (opens at 5 AM) or in the evening — the ceremony of putting Shiva and Meenakshi to bed around 9 PM is an intense experience. Note: no shoes or shorts, and non-Hindus do not have access to the inner sanctum.

After the temple, pop over to the Thirumalai Nayakkar Mahal, a 17th-century palace built by King Thirumalai Nayak in 1636. Only a quarter of the original building survives (the king's grandson dismantled the rest to build a new palace in Trichy), but step into the main hall: its massive 12-metre-high columns give you a sense of past grandeur. A sound and light show takes place in the evening.

activities.text: Madurai's flower market, reached on an excursion from Madurai, is a festival of colours and scents - mountains of jasmine (Madurai's flower), roses and marigolds are piled in baskets. Tamil women wear jasmine garlands in their hair, and the flowers are used as offerings at the temple. Come early in the morning when deliveries arrive.

The Gandhi Memorial Museum, housed in the former Rani Mangammal Palace, traces the Mahatma's life. The most moving exhibit is the bloodstained dhoti Gandhi was wearing when he was assassinated on 30 January 1948. The museum is well curated and free.

Prepare for your journey from Madurai to Rameswaram: express trains link the two cities in 3-4 hours over 170 km. The highlight is Pamban Bridge, which crosses the sea on piers to connect Rameswaram Island to the mainland. The train literally runs above the ocean. Choose a window seat.

visits.text: Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram) has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984. Start with the Shore Temple, built in the 8th century by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II. This granite temple facing the sea is one of the oldest structural stone temples in southern India. Two towers dedicated to Shiva and a shrine to Vishnu stand facing the waves of the Bay of Bengal. Arrive at opening time (6 am) to enjoy the golden morning light and the peace - tourist buses arrive after 9 am.

500 meters south, the Five Rathas (Pancha Rathas) are five monolithic temples each carved from a single granite block in the 7th century. Each bears the name of one of the Pandava brothers from the Mahabharata and illustrates a different architectural style—from simple to complex. It's like a textbook of Indian architecture in stone. In front of the largest ratha, a life-size elephant was carved from the same rock.

Don't miss the bas-relief of Arjuna's Penance (or Descent of the Ganges), a sculptural fresco 27 meters long and 9 meters high carved into a rock face. Hundreds of figures—gods, humans, animals, nagas—converge toward a central fissure representing the Ganges descending from heaven. It's one of the world's largest bas-reliefs. Just beside it, Krishna's Butter Ball is an enormous spherical boulder weighing 250 tonnes balanced on a slope—no one has ever managed to move it, not even the British with their elephants.

activities.text: Late in the day, head to Mahabalipuram beach. Less touristy than Chennai's beaches, it's lined with fishing catamarans and small restaurants where you can eat grilled fish with your feet in the sand. Walk south toward the new fishing harbor to watch boats returning at dusk.

visits.text: The Dharamsala to Manali road is long (about 8 hours) but spectacular—it winds through the Kangra and Kullu valleys, between apple orchards, turquoise rivers, and snowy peaks. Plan stops for the views. Once in Manali, settle in and start with Hadimba Devi Temple, nestled in a cedar forest 2 km from the town center. Built in 1553 by Maharaja Bahadur Singh, it's a four-tiered wooden and stone pagoda temple, dedicated to Hadimba, a demoness from the Mahabharata who became a goddess after marrying the warrior Bhima. The architecture is unique in India—the wooden doors are adorned with detailed carvings of mythological figures.

Climb up to Old Manali, 2 km upstream from the modern town. This stone and wood village has kept its Himalayan charm despite the influx of trendy cafés and guesthouses. Traditional wooden and slate houses cling to the slope, and lanes open onto unobstructed views toward the peaks. This is where the hippie community settled in the 1970s—the vibe remains laid-back.

Detour to Vashisht, a hot-spring village 3 km from Manali. Natural hot springs feed public pools where locals and travelers bathe side by side. The Vashisht temple, dedicated to the Vedic sage of the same name, is a fine example of Himachali wooden architecture with detailed carvings on the lintels.

Your second day in Manali is devoted to the higher elevations. Head to Solang Valley (14 km, 30 min), a natural amphitheater surrounded by snowy peaks. Depending on the season, you'll find paragliding, zorbing, and quad rides (summer), or skiing and sledding (winter). The gondola takes you up to an altitude of 3,000 m with views down into the Kullu Valley. Arrive early—crowds show up after 10 am.

Take the road from Manali to the village of Kothi and allow for a round trip during the day. On the road to Rohtang, this village overlooks a deep gorge carved by the Beas. Stop at the viewpoint beside the road to see the river confined between rocky walls, then explore the village on foot. The houses and wooded slopes form a foreground to the snow-covered peaks. This stop lets you see the valley scenery without going all the way up to the pass. Bring warm clothes for outdoor stops.

If Rohtang is closed, take the Atal Tunnel instead, the longest high-altitude road tunnel in the world (9.02 km), inaugurated in 2020. It connects the Kullu Valley to Lahaul in 30 minutes instead of 4 to 6 hours via the pass. On the other side, the village of Sissu and its waterfall offer a first glimpse of the desert landscapes of Lahaul - a striking contrast with the greenery of Manali. Allow for a round trip during the day from Manali through the Atal Tunnel to visit Sissu.

activities.text: Walk along the Beas River, which runs through the Kullu Valley. In season (May to June, September to October), operators offer white-water rafting between Pirdi and Jhiri - a 14 km stretch with class II to III rapids, perfect for a first experience. Allow for a round trip from Manali to reach the starting point at Pirdi.

Taste Himachali specialties: siddu (steamed bread stuffed with nuts and spices), madra (chickpeas in yogurt sauce), and fresh trout caught from the Beas, grilled or curried. Old Manali restaurants have the best menus.

Late in the day, climb to Manu Temple, dedicated to the sage Manu, regarded in Hindu mythology as humanity's creator—Manali takes its name from him. The temple is modest but the path offers unobstructed valley views.

Try tandem paragliding from Solang Valley or Marhi—Himalayan updrafts carry you above the valley for 15 to 20 minutes. The sensation of soaring with the 6,000-meter mountain range before you is unforgettable. Operators offer the flight with GoPro video included.

Stop at Vashisht hot springs on the way back if you didn't visit them yesterday. After a day at altitude, a bath in naturally hot sulfurous water is the best remedy for fatigue. Locals come at dawn—late in the day you'll have more space.

visits.text: Less well known than Tadoba or Pench, Kawal Tiger Reserve was declared a tiger reserve in 2012. It serves as a corridor between the forests of central India and the Eastern Ghats. The visitor center is in Jannaram; allow a day for the round trip from Mancherial. Leopards, gaur, wolves, and around 300 bird species have been recorded there.

activities.text: You take a short morning safari from Jannaram gate along 15 km of forest track, with observation towers included on the route. Allow a day for the round trip from Mancherial. The official price is around 3,500 rupees per vehicle. Book through the Forest Department; the park closes from July to September for the monsoon.

visits.text: Walk through the 450-acre estate of Vijay Vilas Palace, built between 1920 and 1929 for the son of the Maharao of Kutch. The red sandstone chhatris, jharokas, and jalis evoke the palaces of Rajasthan, but the sea breeze reminds you that the Arabian Sea lies just a few meters away. The royal family still resides on the upper floors. The 2 km private beach below is open to visitors.

The carpenters at Mandvi's port call it “building a boat the old-fashioned way”: solid-wood dhows still emerge from Mandvi's shipyard, built without plans, by eye and with a mallet. This yard is one of the last in Gujarat still building traditional wooden boats for trade in the Persian Gulf. Stop by before 1pm when activity peaks.

activities.text: If time permits, head to Mandvi Beach after visiting the palace: a golden sandy beach. Sunset over the Arabian Sea from this beach is quieter than elsewhere along the coast. Avoid the monsoon, when the waves are dangerous.

visits.text: Medieval astronomers designed Modhera's Sun Temple so that at both equinoxes, the first rays of sun pass straight through the sanctuary without casting a shadow. Built around 1026–27 by King Bhima I of the Solanki dynasty, the temple has no longer been used for worship since the invasions—no rituals are performed here—but this absence preserves a rare purity of form. Arrive when it opens at 8am for the light falling across the friezes at a low angle.

The Surya Kund, a rectangular tank 123 feet long according to archaeological surveys, stands before the temple. Its 108 small shrines, arranged in tiers, are reflected in the water—the symmetry is complete, as is the silence. The tank was used for ritual ablutions before the temple ceased to be used for worship. Don't miss the adjacent museum, open 10am–5pm except Friday.

activities.text: Stay for sunset: the sound-and-light show at Modhera's Sun Temple projects the history of the Solankis onto the carved walls. Artificial light reveals details invisible in daylight—particularly the erotic frieze on the base, often overlooked. Evening shows, with a fee separate from admission (admission: ₹40 for Indians / ₹600 for foreigners in 2026).

visits.text: The drive from Alleppey to Munnar takes 4 to 5 hours, but it's magnificent—you pass from flat paddy fields to the first hills of the Western Ghats, with waterfalls along the way (stop at Cheeyappara if you have time). Munnar sits at 1,600 m altitude, and tea plantations stretch as far as the eye can see across the hills. The first tea bushes were planted here by Scottish planters in the late 19th century. Wander through the rows of tea bushes—the Kannan Devan estate alone covers 24,000 hectares. To really immerse yourself, ask to observe the morning picking (7am–9am), when women in saris move through the fields with their large baskets.

Step into the Munnar Tea Museum (Kannan Devan Tea Museum), 3.5 km from the town center. Inaugurated in 2005 by the Tata Group, it traces the history of the plantations from the days of the British pioneers. You'll see a manual tea roller from 1905, a 1920s Pelton wheel that powered the factories, and a locomotive wheel from the railway that ran between Munnar and Top Station. The museum offers two demonstration sessions per day (10am and 2pm) and a tasting of different teas for a fee. Closed Mondays. Allow 45 minutes to an hour.

Second day in Munnar: head to Mattupetty Dam, 13 km from the town center. This artificial lake surrounded by tea-covered hills and shola forests is one of the region's most beautiful spots. You can take a motorboat tour on the lake, or simply walk along the shore to enjoy the calm. On the way, stop at Echo Point—shout toward the hills and your voice bounces back clearly. It's touristy, but kids love it.

Continue to Kundala Lake, 20 km from Munnar. This high-altitude lake is surrounded by tea plantations and forests. Pedal boats and shikaras (small traditional boats from Kashmir) are available for a leisurely ride. The road there winds through postcard-perfect landscapes—keep your camera ready.

activities.text: Get up before dawn to watch the sunrise from the hills of Munnar. The most spectacular viewpoints are Pothamedu (5 km from the center) and Top Station (32 km away, at 1,880 m; plan a round trip from Munnar). As the mist lifts over the rolling green plantations, the sight is striking. Bring a sweater—at this altitude, mornings are cool, often around 10°C.

If you have the energy, visit Eravikulam National Park, 15 km from Munnar, outside its seasonal closure from February to March. This 97 km² park in the Western Ghats is home to the Nilgiri tahr, an endangered wild goat. Access to the visitor area is by the park's shuttle buses, followed by a walk along the permitted route, approximately 2 km round trip. Every twelve years, these hills are covered in blue neelakurinji flowers—the next bloom is expected in 2030.

Plan a separate excursion from Munnar to stop at Chinnakanal Waterfalls (also called Power House Falls), 18 km from Munnar. The water descends from an altitude of 2,000 m through dense vegetation - a particularly impressive sight after the monsoon. The path to get closer is short but slippery, so wear good shoes.

End the day with a guided jeep tour of a tea plantation. The Lockhart estate, accessible only by 4x4, offers an experience away from the crowds: you drive between rows of tea bushes, watch the manufacturing process in the mini-factory, and taste freshly brewed tea. Book in advance through your accommodation—spaces are limited.

visits.text: Munroe Island is an archipelago of eight islets at the confluence of Ashtamudi Lake and the Kallada River, 25 km from Kollam. Here, there are no crowded houseboats like in Alleppey—you glide in a canoe hollowed out of a tree trunk, maneuvered with a bamboo pole, through channels so narrow that palm fronds brush your shoulders. The island takes its name from Colonel John Munro, a British administrator of Travancore in the 19th century. Book a morning canoe trip lasting 2 to 3 hours: you'll pass through natural mangrove arches, drift past houses on stilts, and cross paths with fishermen setting their nets. This is the peaceful, authentic alternative to the touristy backwaters.

After the canoe ride, explore the village by bicycle—most homestays lend bikes free of charge. The 5 km loop around the island is flat and shaded by coconut palms. You'll pass through coconut plantations and paddy fields, and visit coir-making workshops (coir is coconut fiber). Stop at Edachal bridge to watch fishermen at work, and if you come across a coir workshop, ask for a demonstration—artisans have been hand-braiding the fiber for generations.

activities.text: Late in the day, join a Kerala cooking class at a local home. Your host will show you how to prepare a traditional fish curry with coconut milk, appam (fermented rice pancakes), and aviyal, a mixed vegetable dish typical of Kerala. You'll eat everything served on a banana leaf, sitting on the floor in local style. It's also a chance to taste toddy, a mildly alcoholic drink tapped from coconut palm sap—the local specialty.

visits.text: The Maharaja's Palace in Mysore is one of India's most visited monuments after the Taj Mahal. Built between 1897 and 1912 by the British architect Henry Irwin, it blends Indo-Saracenic, Gothic and Hindu styles. The durbar halls (audience halls) are adorned with gilding, stained glass, carved columns and solid silver doors. The golden throne, made of fig wood plated with 280 kg of gold, is brought out only during the Dasara festival in September or October, depending on the year. Allow 1½ hours for the visit. Please note: you must remove your shoes and cameras are prohibited inside.

After the palace, dive into Devaraja Market, a ten-minute walk away. This covered bazaar, one of Mysore's oldest, overflows with pyramids of flowers (jasmine, roses, marigold), spices, tropical fruits, and silks. Don't leave without trying the crispy dosas from the stalls—Mysore masala dosas, stuffed with spiced potatoes and green chutney, are a local specialty. If you have a sweet tooth, Mysore pak (a ghee and chickpea flour cake) is a classic.

activities.text: On Sundays and public holidays, as well as during Dasara, the palace lights up with 97,000 bulbs at 7pm. The spectacle lasts about an hour and transforms the building into a golden jewel against the night. Even on weekdays, stroll through the illuminated gardens. Arrive 30 minutes early to secure a good spot—crowds can be dense.

If you have time in the afternoon, climb Chamundi Hill (1,065 m), 13 km from the town center. You can drive up or climb the 1,000 steps. Along the way, you'll pass the monolithic Nandi, 5 meters high and carved from a single block of black granite. At the summit, Chamundeshwari Temple offers a panorama over the entire city and surrounding plains.

visits.text: Nagarjunasagar Dam, built on the Krishna between 1955 and 1969, is one of the world's largest masonry dams. It bears the name of Acharya Nagarjuna, founder of Mahayana Buddhism, who taught in this valley. The view from the dam crest over the reservoir is vertiginous.

Nagarjunakonda island is 90% underwater: what remains accessible at the summit is actually the former hilltop where archaeologists relocated stupas, viharas, and Buddhist sculptures from the 1st-3rd centuries CE before flooding. Acharya Nagarjuna himself is said to have taught here, drawing students from Sri Lanka and China. Closed on Fridays.

activities.text: Take the 9:30 or 11:30 ferry from Vijayapuri to Nagarjunakonda Island: the crossing takes approximately 45 minutes across the reservoir. Bring water and a hat: the island is exposed, with no significant shade outside the museum.

11 km from Nagarjunasagar, Ethipothala Falls plunge 21 meters at the confluence of three rivers. A viewing platform overlooks the basin. Less known than the dam, this stop adds 30 minutes to the itinerary and suits children well.

visits.text: On October 14, 1956, Ambedkar and hundreds of thousands of his supporters embraced Buddhism in Nagpur, in this space now known as Deekshabhoomi. The great white marble stupa—22 meters high, 36 in diameter—contains the ashes of Dr. Ambedkar, architect of the Indian Constitution. One million visitors come annually during Dhammachakra Pravartan Din, the anniversary of the conversion. Accessible to all.
Futala Lake comes alive in the late afternoon: joggers, families, vendors selling bhel puri and sugarcane juice. It is Nagpur's most visited urban park. Free entry. A good time to visit: sunset.

activities.text: You finish at Sitabuldi Market, ideal for Nagpur oranges—the region is one of India's major producers. In season (November to January), stalls overflow. Also look for local chiwda and peda. Allow an hour to browse.

visits.text: The road from Aurangabad to Nashik (225 km, 4.5 hours) crosses the Deccan plateau before descending toward the verdant hills of the Nashik valley. Nashik is one of Hinduism's holiest cities—it hosts the Kumbh Mela every 12 years, the world's largest human gathering (tens of millions of pilgrims). The Godavari River, which Hindus consider the "Ganges of the South," flows through the city.

Explore the sacred ghats along the Godavari—Ramkund is the most important, the place where according to tradition Rama bathed during his exile. Pilgrims bathe here to wash away their sins, and this is where funerary ash immersion rites take place. The atmosphere is intense: temple bells, chants, marigold flowers floating on the water, priests in white dhotis.

If time permits, push on to Trimbakeshwar, 30 km from Nashik—one of the 12 Jyotirlinga (Shiva's most sacred temples in India). The current black stone temple, built in the 18th century by Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao, is surrounded by green hills. It's also the source of the Godavari, which rises on Brahmagiri hill just above. The sanctuary interior is reserved for Hindus, but the exterior architecture and atmosphere are worth the visit.

For archaeology enthusiasts, Pandavleni Caves (or Trirashmi) are a complex of 24 Buddhist caves carved between the 3rd century BC and 2nd century AD—among Maharashtra's oldest. Less spectacular than Ajanta, they offer a glimpse of early Buddhist monastic architecture in a peaceful setting.

activities.text: A surprise: Nashik is the “capital of Indian wine.” Its altitude (around 600 m), dry climate and volcanic soils create conditions similar to California's Napa Valley. Several wineries are open to visitors—Sula Vineyards, the pioneer, offers tastings with views of the lake and vines. York Winery and Grover Zampa are other good options; for Grover Zampa, allow for a round trip from Nashik. End the day with a glass of local Chenin Blanc while watching the sunset over the hills—an unexpected contrast with the millennia-old temples visited in the morning.

visits.text: Start with the Red Fort, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007 — its red sandstone walls rise 23 metres high and encircle a 100-hectare complex. Shah Jahan had it built between 1638 and 1648 as the imperial palace of his new capital, Shahjahanabad. Don't miss the Diwan-i-Khas, the Hall of Private Audiences, whose ceiling was once studded with precious stones. Every 15 August, India's Prime Minister hoists the national flag here — you'll spot the podium from the ramparts. Allow at least 1.5 hours, and arrive at opening time (9:30 AM) to beat the crowds.

Jama Masjid is a five-minute walk from the Red Fort - built by Shah Jahan between 1644 and 1656. Its courtyard can accommodate 25,000 worshippers. Climb to the top of the southern minaret (around 40 metres) for a 360° panorama of Old Delhi - you will see the tangled rooftops of Chandni Chowk and, on a clear day, the dome of Parliament in the distance. Remove your shoes at the entrance, and if you are wearing shorts, you will be lent a sarong.

Dive into Chandni Chowk, Delhi's oldest shopping street — Shah Jahan laid it out in 1650. It's a labyrinth of alleyways where spices, fabrics, jewellery and electronics jostle for space. Make your way to Paranthe Wali Gali, a cul-de-sac famous for its paranthas fried in ghee — there have been stalls here since the 1870s. Fair warning: the crowds are dense, so keep your belongings close.

Make a detour to Raj Ghat, Gandhi's memorial — a slab of black marble marks the spot where he was cremated on 31 January 1948, one day after his assassination. The site is simple and moving, surrounded by lawns. An eternal flame burns here at all times. Allow 30 minutes, barefoot on the marble.

Head to New Delhi this morning — start with Humayun's Tomb, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993. Built in 1570, it's the first great Mughal garden-tomb and the direct blueprint for the Taj Mahal, built 60 years later. The white marble dome stands 42 metres tall, surrounded by symmetrical gardens divided into squares (the Persian charbagh layout). Arrive early in the morning — the golden light on the red sandstone is stunning, and you'll have the place almost to yourself before 10 AM.

You can't miss the Qutub Minar — this 72.5-metre brick tower is the tallest minaret in the world made from this material. Construction began in 1192 under Qutb ud-Din Aibak, Delhi's first sultan, and was completed by his successor Iltutmish. Look closely at the Arabic inscriptions that cover the tower from base to top — each floor features a different balcony style. You can no longer climb to the top (closed after an accident in 1981), but the base is impressive. Right next to it, stop by the 4th-century Iron Pillar that has resisted rust for 1,600 years — a metallurgical mystery no one has cracked yet.

India Gate, Delhi's triumphal arch, stands 42 metres tall. It honours the 70,000 Indian soldiers who died during World War I. In the evening, the monument is lit up and the esplanade becomes a place for families to stroll. It's a good spot for a midday break.

Finish at Lodi Gardens, a 36-hectare park that houses 15th-century tombs from the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties — octagonal buildings set amid immaculate lawns. Delhiites come here to jog or picnic. If you have time, seek out the Tomb of Mohammed Shah (1450) and the Bara Gumbad Mosque.

Back in Delhi — full circle. If you arrive on the morning Vande Bharat Express, you have the afternoon free. Visit what you missed on Days 1–2: the Akshardham Temple (2005) is a spectacular modern complex covering 40 hectares on the banks of the Yamuna — 20,000 statues carved in pink sandstone and white marble. Admission is free but security checks are strict (no phones or cameras allowed inside).

Hauz Khas Village, in south Delhi, centres on a 14th-century reservoir (built by Alauddin Khalji) surrounded by medieval ruins — now reimagined as a trendy quarter with art galleries, designer boutiques and rooftop restaurants. The ruins of the madrasa and the tomb of Firoz Shah Tughlaq overlook the lake — a peaceful and photogenic spot.

activities.text: Take a cycle-rickshaw ride through the alleyways of Old Delhi — it's the best way to weave between market stalls and sacred cows. Negotiate the fare before hopping on (expect around 30–45 minutes for a full tour of the neighbourhood). Pass the Gurudwara Sis Ganj Sahib, a 17th-century Sikh temple you can enter freely and even have a free lunch at the langar, the communal kitchen.

In the evening, if you still have energy, catch the Red Fort's sound and light show — the 45-minute spectacle traces Mughal history with the illuminated walls as a backdrop. The English show starts around 8:30 PM (check times on-site, as they change with the season).

In the late afternoon, walk to the Dargah of Hazrat Nizamuddin — Delhi's most revered Sufi shrine, founded in the 14th century. Every Thursday evening, musicians perform qawwali in the courtyard — the atmosphere is electric, somewhere between devotion and trance. Arrive around 6 PM to settle in before the crowd thickens.

Get ready for your departure to Agra tomorrow morning: the Gatiman Express leaves Hazrat Nizamuddin station at 8:10 AM and arrives at Agra Cantonment at 9:50 AM — that's 100 minutes for 188 km, making it one of India's fastest trains. Book your tickets on IRCTC at least 3–4 days ahead. AC Chair Car is recommended. Note: this train does not run on Fridays.

Last-minute shopping at Khan Market or Connaught Place — for souvenirs, spices, tea, textiles. Khan Market is Delhi's most upscale shopping area, with excellent bookshops and cafés. Connaught Place (CP) is a circle of white colonnades built in 1933 — more down-to-earth, livelier, with the metro right below.

Farewell dinner — Delhi is the gastronomic capital of North India. Butter chicken (invented here in the 1950s), chole bhature, Old Delhi kebabs, Nizamuddin biryani. Thirty days of travel, thousands of kilometres of track, and India stays unpredictable, intense and intense right through to the final meal.

visits.text: You walk along Vodarevu Beach, a quiet beach near Chirala that few foreign travelers know. Allow a day for the round trip from Ongole. The sand is clean, the sea is calmer than in Vizag, and fishing nets drying on the shore set the scene. An ideal stop between Tirupati and Vijayawada for some fresh air. There are no major tourist facilities—that is its appeal.

visits.text: A long drive from Agra (about 7 hours), but Orchha is worth every kilometer. This city founded in the 16th century by Rajput chief Rudra Pratap Singh, on the banks of the Betwa, is one of central India's hidden gems. A UNESCO World Heritage candidate, it has kept a charm that Jaipur or Udaipur lost long ago. Start with Jehangir Mahal, built by King Bir Singh Deo to welcome Mughal emperor Jahangir. Its circular towers, fluted domes, and jali balconies blend Mughal and Rajput styles with rare elegance. Climb to the roof—the view over the river and cenotaphs is sumptuous.

Right next door, the older Raja Mahal preserves wall frescoes of surprising beauty for a building of this era. Peacocks, elephants, and geometric motifs dance across the Darbar Hall walls. Narrow passages and spiral staircases add to the feeling of exploration - you often have rooms to yourself.

Walk down to the cenotaphs (chhatris) along the Betwa - 14 funerary monuments honoring Bundela kings, built on high stone platforms with panchayatan-style domes. Their reflection in the river water at sunset is one of India's most photogenic images. Climb to the top of Bir Singh Deo's cenotaph for a panorama over all of Orchha. Bonus: a colony of long-billed vultures (critically endangered species) nests in the structures.

Visit Ram Raja Temple, India's only temple where Rama is worshiped as a king rather than a god. Uniformed guards render him military honors every day. The neighboring Chaturbhuj temple offers magnificent views from its accessible roof, and Laxmi Narayan temple (1662) preserves detailed wall frescoes on its interior walls.

activities.text: Attend the Jehangir Mahal sound and light show in the evening, which traces Bundela dynasty history. The palaces illuminated at night create a magical atmosphere.
Rent a bicycle and tour Orchha at your own pace - the town is compact enough to explore everything by pedaling. Paths along the Betwa cross bucolic landscapes with palaces in the background.

visits.text: Built in 1213, this UNESCO temple bears its sculptor Ramappa's name—the only temple in India so named. The bricks of its pyramidal tower, called 'floating,' are so porous they rest on water: a Kakatiya technique to lighten roofs. The sculpted pillars show dancers in motion who seem lifted from a Bharatanatyam manual.

Laknavaram Lake stretches across 13 floating islands formed by vegetation accumulating on submerged land, the result of a dam built by the Kakatiyas in the 13th century. The water and wooded hills merge on the horizon. The Telangana state resort rents cottages built on stilts above the lake. Allow for a round trip from Palampet.

activities.text: Cross the 160-meter suspension bridge linking the shore to the islands of Laknavaram Lake: a cable footbridge built in 2016, narrow enough to feel the water swaying beneath your feet. Boat rental is available (50 rupees per adult). The last boat leaves at 5:30 p.m. Allow for a round trip from Palampet.

visits.text: A plateau of white marble in the sky: Shatrunjaya Hill carries over 800 Jain temples built between the 11th and 20th centuries—the complex is one of the two most sacred sites in Jainism along with Shikharji. The temple city is organized into nine tunks (fortified enclosures), and no one is allowed to spend the night there, not even priests. The temples close at noon and do not reopen in the afternoon.

activities.text: Begin the 3,500-step ascent before dawn if you want to reach the summit before the noon closure. Jain pilgrims make the climb barefoot; palankis (sedan chairs) are available for those with limited mobility. At the top, the four-faced Adinath Temple (Chaumukh) dominates the entire Bhavnagar plain. Return by the same path; allow 3 hours for the round trip.

places.name: Palolem

visits.text: Arrival in Palolem, southern Goa - and the contrast with Hampi is striking. It's a 1.6 km crescent bay of white sand lined with coconut palms, with shallow water ideal for swimming. A former fishing village turned traveler spot, Palolem maintains a laid-back atmosphere compared to north Goa. Settle into one of the beach huts and enjoy this first day with your toes in the sand.

Late afternoon, walk south along the beach to Patnem Beach - an even quieter cove, separated from Palolem by a rocky headland (10 minutes' walk). Patnem is smaller, with fewer shacks but an almost meditative atmosphere. The water is clear and the sandy bottom slopes gently.

Excursion to Cabo de Rama Fort, perched on a headland overlooking the Arabian Sea. Its name comes from the Ramayana - Rama and Sita are said to have stayed here during their exile. The fort existed well before the Portuguese, who took it in 1763 from the Raja of Soonda and fortified it with a chapel dedicated to Saint Anthony. It served as a prison from 1935 to 1955. Today in ruins, there remain rusted cannons on the bastions and the small white church. Entry is free - push to the western edge for a vertiginous view over the cliffs and ocean.

Coming down from the fort, detour to Cola Beach - an isolated beach accessible by dirt track. Cola's special feature is its freshwater lagoon just behind the beach, separated from the sea by a sand spit. The contrast between the lagoon's blue water and the Arabian Sea waves is striking. Few people, no noisy shacks - this is secret Goa.

Take a local bus or taxi to Margao (Madgaon), the capital of south Goa, 40 km away. The town retains a strong Portuguese imprint: colonial houses in pastel facades line the old quarter. Step through the door of the Church of the Holy Spirit, built in 1675 - its white baroque facade dominates the central square, and the interior contains a remarkable gilded altarpiece.

Margao Municipal Market is a festival for the senses: mountains of spices (pepper, cinnamon, cardamom), fresh fish spread on ice, unknown tropical fruits. It's the busiest market in south Goa - go in the morning when the stalls are full. Count on a good hour to tour it without rushing.

activities.text: Take a kayak from the northern end of Palolem to reach Butterfly Beach - a cove accessible only by sea or jungle trail. You can see butterflies between October and March, and the beach is rarely crowded. The kayak crossing takes 15-20 minutes - it's also a chance to spot dolphins early in the morning.

Sunset at Palolem faces west: the sun descends between the bay's two rocky headlands. This is when the shacks light candles and fishermen pull up their colorful boats. Stay for dinner - the grilled catch of the day with kokum curry (local sour fruit) is the local specialty.

The south Goa coastal road between Palolem and Cabo de Rama (about 20 km) passes through fishing villages, coconut groves and viewpoints over coves. By scooter, it's a treat - stop whenever a view tempts you. Fill up with petrol before leaving, there are no stations between the two.

If you have time on the return, make a detour to Agonda Beach - a long beach less crowded than Palolem, lined with palms and a few wooden cabanas. The vibe is very relaxed, with possibilities for yoga and ayurveda in centers set up along the beach.

If timing allows, head down to Colva Beach - a huge white sand beach very popular with Goans on weekends. The contrast with the southern coves is clear: here it's livelier, with shacks lined up and a family atmosphere. Count on 15 minutes by taxi from Margao.

Prepare departure to Kochi: from Madgaon (Margao station), the Mangala Lakshadweep Express or Netravati Express connect to Ernakulam Junction (Kochi) in 10-14 hours depending on the train. Overnight journeys are ideal - you save a day. Book your berth in advance via IRCTC.

visits.text: An engineering marvel: at Panagal's Chaya Someshwara Temple, built in the 11th-12th centuries by the Cholas of Kunduru, a pillar's shadow perpetually falls on the Shiva Lingam, from sunrise to sunset. No trickery: architects simply calculated the angle precisely. The temple is a Trikutalayam dedicated to Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva.

Locals say that Pachala Someswara means “Lord Someswara of the green onyx”: the deity is carved from green onyx stone, which is rare in the subcontinent. This second temple in Panagal, 1 km from the first, has more sophisticated sculpture and fewer visitors. The adjoining archaeological museum is open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. except on Fridays.
