visits.text: Seven stories below ground, yet Rani ki Vav is a temple. UNESCO listed it in 2014, describing it as “the most developed and most ornate” of India's stepwells. Built in the 11th century by Queen Udayamati as a memorial to her husband, King Bhima I, it features over 500 principal sculptures and more than 1,000 secondary ones. Its image has appeared on the reverse of 100-rupee notes since 2019.

Cotton stretched on handlooms, the steady quiver of threads, the smell of natural dye: this is Patan's Patola House, one of the few workshops still weaving patola, a double-ikat sari in which each thread is dyed before weaving. A quality sari can take two weavers six months to make. The workshops can be visited; purchases are possible on site, but prices reflect the time invested.

activities.text: Patan was Gujarat's medieval capital before Ahmedabad—the old town retains weavers' quarters within walking distance of Rani ki Vav. Follow the lanes of Siddhapur Mohalla where family workshops sell embroidered textiles and silks directly. Less touristy than the fitted-out shops, Patan's bazaar gives a sense of the commercial fabric that made this city wealthy.

activities.text: Since the reign of the Kakatiyas, Pembarthi’s artisans have worked brass by hand on sheets ten thousandths thick - no machines, no molds. The village of Pembarthi is now home to a handful of families who preserve this GI-certified craft. Stop for 20 to 30 minutes to watch a piece being embossed.

visits.text: The real Jungle Book forests are here, in Pench Tiger Reserve. The 758 km² reserve inspired Kipling through William Henry Sleeman's writings about a wolf-child captured in 1831 near Seoni. The park now bears the name Indira Priyadarshini Pench National Park, and its sanctuary the name Mowgli Pench Sanctuary. Turia Gate is the most popular for safaris.

activities.text: Kipling never visited Pench, but the Seoni valley, the banks of the Waingunga River, and the village of Kanhiwara he describes in the novel actually exist. Your guide can identify these landmarks in the forest. The interpretation of this literary connection, offered at the Turia center since 2006, is surprisingly well documented.

If luck is on your side at dawn, a tiger on the Pench trail regards you with royal indifference—and walks away. Morning safaris (6–9am) in the Turia or Karmajhiri zone offer the best chances. Besides tigers: leopards, sloth bears, nilgais, and wild dogs.

visits.text: Bhoodan Pochampally, the 'silk village of the Deccan,' received the UNWTO Best Tourism Village label in 2021 and GI status in 2004 for its double ikat—a technique of dyeing threads before weaving. A complex saree can take several weeks to complete. Park at the village entrance and walk in to see looms in action.

activities.text: Silk threads braided before dyeing create geometric patterns that seem to float in the finished fabric. Visit a family workshop to witness the resist process: sections to be dyed are tied by hand, thread by thread. Direct purchase from the workshop, no middleman.

visits.text: On October 2, 1869, in this three-story ancestral house purchased by Gandhi's great-grandfather, Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born. Kirti Mandir is the memorial built in 1950 against the original facade: the room where he was born is visible behind glass, and the spinning wheel and low desk have been faithfully recreated. Free entry; open 9am–6pm daily.

activities.text: The neighborhood around Kirti Mandir, where heads are bowed and lanes are narrow, reveals Gandhi's city better than the museum: merchants selling bandhani at ₹300 per piece, grocers selling papads and sev typical of Saurashtra, and Kasturba's birthplace—Navi Khadi—a hundred meters away. A round trip on foot through these lanes takes thirty minutes.

places.name: Puducherry

visits.text: Train from Thanjavur → Puducherry via Trichy (about 4–5 hours with a connection). Puducherry (formerly Pondicherry) is the former French trading post in India — handed over by France in 1954. The French Quarter (Ville Blanche) is a grid of quiet streets lined with mustard-yellow colonial houses, bougainvillea spilling from balconies and street signs in French. Rue Suffren, Rue Dumas, Rue Romain Rolland — you could almost forget you're in India. Except the sacred cows haven't read the street names.

Walk down to Promenade Beach, which runs 1.5 km along the Bay of Bengal — an esplanade flanked by colonial buildings, a Gandhi statue and the French war memorial. Cars are banned in the morning and evening, making for a pleasant stroll. At the northern end, spot the old lighthouse and Bharathi Park.

The Sri Aurobindo Ashram, in the heart of the French Quarter, is the spiritual centre around which Puducherry has built its identity since the 1920s. Sri Aurobindo, philosopher and independence activist, settled here in 1910 to escape the British police. The ashram now occupies several buildings — the samadhi (tomb) of Sri Aurobindo and the Mother, covered in flowers, sits at the centre of a silent courtyard. Admission is free and open to all, but silence is expected.

Paradise Beach, accessible only by boat from Chunnambar Boat House (a 15-minute crossing on the backwaters), is a strip of sand between the river and the sea. Wilder than Promenade Beach, it is lined with casuarinas and almost deserted on weekdays.

activities.text: Take an excursion to Auroville, 12 km from Puducherry — a “universal city” founded in 1968 by Mirra Alfassa (“The Mother”), the spiritual companion of Sri Aurobindo. The Matrimandir, a golden sphere 29 metres in diameter at the community's centre, is the iconic image of the place. Visiting the Matrimandir requires advance booking — without it, you'll only see the outer garden. Around 3,000 people of 60 nationalities live in Auroville.

Dinner in the Tamil Quarter (Ville Noire) for a striking contrast with the French side — dosa and idli in the morning, chettinad at lunch, and French crêpes in the evening. Puducherry is the only city in India where you can switch between a café au lait and a filter coffee without crossing a border.

Rent a bicycle and explore the French Quarter and its surroundings — it's the best way to get around Puducherry. The streets are flat and distances short. Swing by Goubert Market (near the beach) for tropical fruits and flowers.

Get ready for your Puducherry → Chennai journey: trains connect the two cities in about 3.5 hours for 150 km. The Villupuram–Chennai Express is a daily option. You can also take an air-conditioned Volvo bus (3 hours direct). Book on IRCTC.

visits.text: The drive from Lonavala to Pune is short (65 km, 1.5 hours). Pune, Maharashtra's second city, was the former capital of the Maratha Empire—the one that stood up to both the Mughals and the British. Start with Shaniwar Wada, the fortified palace of the Peshwas (Maratha prime ministers), built in 1732. A mysterious fire in 1828 destroyed almost everything—only the imposing perimeter walls and massive gates remain. The Delhi Gate, the main entrance, bristles with 72 steel spikes designed to prevent war elephant charges. The contrast between the grandeur of the ruins and the emptiness inside is striking—imagine this palace at its peak, when the Peshwas ruled an empire stretching from southern to northern India.

Next, visit Aga Khan Palace, an elegant 1892 building surrounded by gardens, whose history is inseparable from India's independence struggle. The British imprisoned Gandhi, his wife Kasturba, and his secretary Mahadev Desai here from 1942 to 1944, during the "Quit India" movement. Kasturba died here on February 22, 1944—a memorial and samadhi (cremation site) mark the spot in the gardens. The museum inside traces Gandhi's life through photographs, letters, and personal objects. The atmosphere is emotionally charged.

For Indian craft enthusiasts, the Raja Dinkar Kelkar Museum houses a staggering collection of 20,000 art objects assembled by one man over his lifetime: musical instruments, ornate locks, oil lamps, weapons, carved doors, palanquins. It's a cabinet of Indian curiosities that makes your head spin.

activities.text: Pune is a dynamic student city—spend the evening exploring the Koregaon Park neighborhood, with its cafés, restaurants, and bars. The culinary scene is diverse: from traditional Maharashtrian restaurants to trendy cafés. Try misal pav—Pune's signature dish, a spicy sprouted pea curry served with brioche-style bread, topped with farsan (crunchy garnish).

visits.text: Although closed to non-Hindus, the Jagannath Temple remains an imposing presence in the city. Built in the 12th century by Anantavarman Chodaganga, the temple can feed more than 100,000 people a day through its ritual kitchen.

The black sand of Puri Beach burns underfoot at noon—a sign of its dark mineral content. A long, lively beach with fishermen hauling nets by hand, riders offering horseback rides, and a row of hotels in the background. A walk is recommended early in the morning or at sunset.

activities.text: Devotees consider Mahaprasad, the temple's sacred food, the purest meal in India—regardless of who prepares or eats it. Ananda Bazaar is inside the Jagannath Temple compound, which is closed to non-Hindus. If you cannot enter, look for Mahaprasad in the shops outside the temple: rice, vegetable curry, and khichdi.

visits.text: Pushkar Lake is one of Hinduism's few sacred lakes—according to legend, it was created when Brahma dropped a lotus petal to earth. Its 52 ghats (sacred steps) descend to the water where pilgrims bathe and make flower offerings. Remove your shoes when approaching the ghats and be discreet—this is a place of prayer, not a photo backdrop. Beware fake priests who insist on tying a red thread to your wrist then demand a 'donation.'

Pushkar's Brahma Temple is one of the very rare temples worldwide dedicated to Brahma, the creator god. The entrance is marked by a marble gate and the floor is paved with silver tiles. The temple is small but the fervor of devotees is intense. Opens at 6am—go early to avoid the queues.

Climb to the Savitri Temple, perched on the hill overlooking Pushkar. The walk up takes 30-40 minutes (a cable car also exists). From the summit, the view over the lake, temples and surrounding dunes is Pushkar's finest, especially at sunrise or sunset.

Wander through the lanes of Pushkar bazaar—a surprising mix of hippie souvenir shops, incense stalls and street food stands. Pushkar is a vegetarian town (no alcohol or meat in the town center restaurants) due to its sacred character. Try malpua, a local sweet fried pancake, the town's specialty.

activities.text: If your trip coincides with Holi (February or March, depending on the year), Pushkar is one of India's major centers for the festival of colors. Celebrations around the lake are supervised and very festive—bring clothes you can sacrifice and protect your cameras with a waterproof bag.

visits.text: From the ghats of Rajahmundry, the Godavari is so wide—5 to 6 km at this point—you'd think you were seeing an inland sea. The city is a center of Telugu culture from which artists and poets who shaped Andhra have emerged. The ghats come alive early in the morning, with ritual baths and flower vendors. The river view at sunset is unobstructed.

activities.text: The cruise to Papikondalu is a leisurely luxury: the Godavari, several kilometers wide at Rajahmundry, gradually narrows to 150 meters as it enters the gorges of the Papi Hills, a densely forested area between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. The journey takes a full day, departing from Polavaram. Book the day before.

visits.text: The Ramanathaswamy Temple is one of the four Char Dham, the most sacred pilgrimage sites in Hinduism. According to legend, this is where Rama prayed to Shiva to purify himself after killing the demon king Ravana. The temple possesses the longest corridors of any Hindu temple in the world—197 meters bordered by 1,212 sculpted granite columns. Inside, 22 sacred wells (theerthams) represent the 22 arrows from Rama's quiver. Pilgrims are sprinkled with water from each well—each is said to cure a different ailment. Allow a minimum of 2 hours and leave your cameras outside.

Before reaching Rameswaram, you will cross the Pamban road bridge, which connects the island to the mainland over the Palk Strait. The Pamban Bridge built in 1914 is a railway structure separate from the road crossing. As you cross the strait, admire the turquoise ocean on either side and the view of the neighboring railway structures before entering the island.

Push on to Dhanushkodi, 20 km east of Rameswaram—the extreme eastern tip of the Indian subcontinent. This ghost village was destroyed by a cyclone in 1964 that killed more than 1,800 people. Only the ruins of a church and railway station remain, engulfed by sand. At the end of the track, you'll see the sandbanks of Adam's Bridge (Rama Setu), that alignment of shoals extending toward Sri Lanka 30 km away. The place is otherworldly and striking—go in the morning to avoid the heat.

activities.text: The ritual bathing at Agni Theertham, the sacred beach facing the temple, is a spectacle in itself. Pilgrims immerse themselves in the ocean before entering the temple. Even if you don't practice the rite, the beach at sunrise, with the fishermen and devotees, offers a powerful moment in your journey.

Wander through Rameswaram's colorful alleys in late afternoon. The flower stalls, seashell vendors, and chai shops create the atmosphere of a pilgrimage town, very different from tourist beach resorts. The sunset on the island's western shoreline, facing the mainland, is peaceful.

visits.text: Rishikesh - the 'world capital of yoga' - sits where the Ganges leaves the Himalayan foothills for the plains. The atmosphere is radically different from Delhi's chaos: here cows, sadhus in orange, and backpackers in yoga pants coexist on the ghats. Start by crossing Ram Jhula, the 137-meter suspension bridge built in 1986, linking ashrams on both banks. The view of the turquoise Ganges, framed by forested hills, sets the tone.

Visit the Beatles Ashram (officially Chaurasi Kutia), Maharishi Mahesh Yogi's former ashram where John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr stayed in 1968 to study Transcendental Meditation. Abandoned for decades, the site has reopened to visitors and the ruined buildings are covered with colorful graffiti and murals honoring the Fab Four. They composed much of the White Album here. The place is strangely peaceful despite its fame.

Walk down to Swarg Ashram, the pedestrian quarter on the Ganges' left bank. No cars here—only lanes lined with ashrams, temples, and small vegetarian restaurants. Bharat Mandir, Rishikesh's oldest temple, is dedicated to Vishnu and is believed to date from the 12th century.

Late in the day, head to Triveni Ghat or Parmarth Niketan for Ganga Aarti—the evening ceremony where dozens of priests wave large oil lamps while facing the river as mantras resound. Hundreds of small floating lamps (diyas) are placed on the water. The atmosphere is intense and deeply moving—arrive 30 minutes early to find a good spot on the steps.

activities.text: Go rafting on the Ganges—Rishikesh is India's number one spot for this activity. Several routes from 9 to 36 km are available, with class II to IV rapids. The classic Shivpuri to Rishikesh stretch (16 km, 3–4 hours) passes through the “Roller Coaster” and “Golf Course” rapids. Book the day before with local operators.

Take a one- or two-hour yoga class at one of the countless ashrams. Even if you've never practiced, this is the ideal place to start—beginner classes are everywhere. The International Yoga Festival takes place every March at Parmarth Niketan.

visits.text: The Great Stupa of Sanchi, begun in the 3rd century BCE under Ashoka, is one of India's oldest stone monuments. Set on a quiet hill 50 km from Bhopal, it stands 16 meters tall and 36 in diameter. Its four sculpted gateways (toranas), added after Ashoka's death, recount episodes from the Buddha's life without ever representing him in human form. UNESCO since 1989.

You visit the museum to see the capital of Ashoka's pillar, a copy of the Lion Capital that is India's official emblem. Sanchi's original is here, in this austere museum at the foot of the hill. Open daily except Fridays.

activities.text: In the evening, the sculpted gates take on a honey color under the low light, and tourists thin out. This is the time to circle the balustrade in silence, read the reliefs without jostling. Sri Lankan pilgrims regularly make the journey here. Walking clockwise around the stupa is the classic ritual gesture.

visits.text: The prison says: “Pay 500 rupees, become an inmate.” The Heritage Jail Museum in Sangareddy, built in 1796 under the administration of Nizam Prime Minister Salar Jung I, is the country’s first prison museum. For 500 rupees, you put on the khaki uniform, eat the prison ration and sleep in a barracks. Booking is recommended.

visits.text: Gir National Park, 1,412 km² of deciduous forest in Saurashtra, is home to the Asiatic lion (Panthera leo persica). The population has grown from fewer than twenty individuals in the early 20th century to more than 600 today according to Responsible Travel. A remarkable recovery - and still a precarious one.

activities.text: The morning safari is the only time that counts: between 6am and 9am, lions are active, the light is soft, and guides know where the prides pass through. Advance booking is mandatory, well ahead of your visit in high season (November–March), through the Gujarat forest portal. Devalia Safari Park, a fenced area within the park, guarantees close-range sightings.

If the lions keep a low profile, the rest of Gir has some pleasant surprises in store: over 300 bird species, leopards, mugger crocodiles in the rivers, jackals, and sambar deer. The forest is also inhabited by the Maldharis, a pastoral community that has coexisted with lions for generations. Local guides tell their stories.

visits.text: India's first Ramsar-listed salt lake, designated in 1981—Chilika Lake spans roughly 1,100 km² during the rainy season, shrinking to 900 km² in the dry season. This brackish lagoon, fed by 52 rivers and opening onto the Bay of Bengal, nearly died from illegal aquaculture in the 1990s. The opening of a new marine outlet in 2000 saved it. Embark from Satapada for the dolphin cruise.

Nalabana is an officially protected bird sanctuary in the heart of Chilika Lake. In winter, dozens of migratory species arrive from Siberia, Central Asia and the Caspian basin: flamingos, pelicans and egrets. Birdwatching takes place from a boat outside the protected perimeter; visitors are not allowed to land on the island.

activities.text: A saltwater dolphin in a semi-enclosed lake—the Irrawaddy dolphin (Orcaella brevirostris) of Chilika is a gentle anomaly. This round-snouted cetacean lives mainly around the lake's mouth at Satapada. The cruise lasts 2 to 3 hours; government operators are more reliable than private ones. Season: year-round, but calm waters from October to March facilitate sightings.

If you come between November and February, flamingos and migratory ducks by the thousands settle at Nalabana. It's not an organized spectacle—just look left. Binoculars essential. Avoid weekends if you want tranquility.

visits.text: Ranthambore Fort perches 213 meters above the forest, at the heart of the national park—the only major Indian fort located entirely within a tiger reserve. Founded around 944 by Chauhan king Sapaldaksha, a UNESCO site since 2013, it changed hands about ten times over the centuries. Climb the 273 steps to the summit to discover the Trinetra Ganesh temple—the world's only one where Ganesh is depicted with three eyes. Langurs populate the ruins, and occasionally a tiger prowls below. The view over the park from the ramparts is spectacular.

On a safari whose route passes Padam Talao and the Raj Bagh ruins, view these sites from the vehicle: walking around the lakes is not permitted. The lakes are home to crocodiles basking in the sun, sambar deer and troops of langurs. The area is rich in birds—purple herons, serpent eagles and kingfishers. Bring binoculars.

activities.text: Dawn jeep safari in Ranthambore National Park. The 392 km² park shelters around 70 Bengal tigers—a rare trait: they're diurnal, which increases the odds of spotting them in broad daylight. The 6-seater jeep safari lasts 3 hours. Book online several weeks ahead—zones 2, 3 and 4 offer the best chances. Bring warm layers for the winter morning, and keep your eyes on the langurs: their alarm call often betrays a nearby cat.

days_plan.itin_title: Intensive Rajasthan Road Trip: Forts, Tigers & Taj Mahal

visits.text: Somnath Temple juts out toward the Arabian Sea as if defying the horizon. First of Shiva's twelve Jyotirlingas, it has been destroyed and rebuilt multiple times throughout history—the current structure dates from 1951, rebuilt in Chalukya style at Sardar Patel's instigation. The evening aarti at dusk, against a backdrop of waves, is a moment of great intensity. Avoid festival days: crowds are uncontrollable.

Triveni Sangam marks the confluence of the Hiran, Kapila and mythical Saraswati rivers - a sacred site for ritual bathing since antiquity according to government texts from Gir Somnath District. Bhalka Tirth is the place where, according to tradition, Krishna is said to have left the earthly world.

activities.text: Attend the evening aarti: drums, conches, and chants resonate in the main hall as light fades over the sea. The temple opens at 6am and closes at 10pm. Non-Hindus are allowed access, but entry to the inner areas is restricted at certain times; check at the entrance.

days_plan.itin_title: Gujarat: Grand Tour of UNESCO Sites in 15 Days

visits.text: Pink silhouettes stand out against the calm water long before you make out the flamingos. Pulicat Lake, India's second-largest brackish lake according to Wikipedia, stretches between Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh along the road to the space center. In winter, migratory birds from Siberia settle here for the season. The best viewing point sits on the Sriharikota causeway: no boat needed. Visit between November and February.

Here, 105 kilometers north of Chennai, India sends its rockets into space. The Satish Dhawan Space Centre is ISRO's main spaceport, established on the island of Sriharikota in the 1970s. The viewing gallery lets visitors watch scheduled launches, with advance registration through ISRO. The Rocket Garden and the other Space Theme Park facilities are not yet open to the public. Do not plan an independent visit to the space center; check entry requirements before traveling there.

activities.text: You drive along the Sriharikota causeway at sunrise with the windows down: flocks of pelicans and painted storks cross the waters of Pulicat on either side at this hour. You can stop freely; no ticket is required.

days_plan.itin_title: India's East Coast: Chennai to Visakhapatnam, 13 Days

visits.text: You might expect just another temple, but you find one of India's rare sun temples. Arasavalli Suryanarayana Swamy Temple, built in the 7th century by Kalinga rulers, is oriented so the first rays of sunlight fall directly on the deity's feet twice a year. Popular for its supposed ability to heal skin diseases. The Ratha Saptami festival in February draws large crowds.

activities.text: You visit Arasavalli Suryanarayana Swamy Temple early in the morning to observe devotees in front of the sanctuary and listen to the bells. The morning atmosphere, with incense and bells, is very different from the tourist atmosphere later in the day.

days_plan.itin_title: From Coast to Jungle: Bhubaneswar to Bhopal in 16 Days

visits.text: Thirty-six kilometers from Tirupati, Srikalahasti often takes second place to Tirumala—unfairly. This temple dedicated to Shiva, whose gopuram was enlarged in 1516 under Krishnadevaraya of the Vijayanagara kingdom, is one of the five Pancha Bhoota Sthalas and represents the element of air (Vayu). The name comes from Sri (spider), Kala (serpent), and Hasti (elephant)—three legendary devotees of Shiva. Closed roughly between 1 p.m. and 4 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: India's East Coast: Chennai to Visakhapatnam, 13 Days

visits.text: Created in 1955, Tadoba Andhari is Maharashtra's oldest and largest national park, covering 1,727 km². Dry deciduous forest, a central lake, marshy areas—a varied ecosystem that supports more than 90 tigers according to the park's official website. Besides tigers, dholes (Indian wild dogs) hunt in packs and gaur (Indian bison) cross the clearings. Book safaris well in advance.

Tadoba Lake gleams at dusk, mugger crocodiles move along the banks, and herons perch on dead branches. This central body of water is a hotspot: the need to drink brings all the animals out. The lake is accessible from several park gates; ask your guide which zone is most active that day.

activities.text: The morning safari at Moharli Gate gives you the best chance of seeing a tiger: the light is soft, animals are on the move, and tracks left overnight on the trail are still fresh. The jeep safari lasts about 3 hours. Places are limited—online booking is mandatory.

In summer, heat exceeds 40°C—but it's paradoxically the best season for tigers, who gather around water holes. From March to June, sightings increase as vegetation thins. Evening safari recommended for leopards and sloth bears.

days_plan.itin_title: From Coast to Jungle: Bhubaneswar to Bhopal in 16 Days

visits.text: Before leaving the region, make a detour to Auroville, 12 km north of Puducherry. This “universal city”, founded in 1968 by “the Mother”, brings together around 3,500 residents of 60 nationalities. The Matrimandir—a golden sphere 29 meters in diameter covered in gold disks—is the most photographed building in Tamil Nadu after the temples. You cannot enter the sphere without booking in advance, but you can see it from the outdoor viewpoints accessible from the Visitors' Centre. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes on site.

Get back on the road toward Thanjavur (175 km, roughly 4 hours). The Cauvery plain you'll cross is Tamil Nadu's rice bowl—paddy fields stretching to the horizon, dotted with village temples and their colorful gopurams. Arrive in late afternoon for an initial visit to the Brihadisvara Temple, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1987. Built in just seven years (1003–1010) by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I, it's the largest all-granite temple in India. The main tower (vimana) rises 66 meters—the capstone weighs 80 tonnes and is said to have been hoisted via a 6 km ramp. Visit at the end of the day for the low-angle light on the granite.

activities.text: Before leaving Auroville, browse the craft shops at the Visitors' Centre—pottery, incense, organic cotton clothing. It's the most interesting place to buy local handicrafts in the Puducherry region.

If you reach Thanjavur before closing time, soak up the evening ritual atmosphere at Brihadisvara: priests light oil lamps and chanting echoes beneath the granite vaults. The monolithic Nandi (Shiva's sacred bull), carved from a single 6-meter block, stands guard at the entrance—devotees touch its horns to receive blessings.

Tamil Nadu and Kerala Road Trip: Temples and Backwaters

visits.text: The road from Rameswaram to Thekkady (roughly 300 km, 7–8 hours) crosses the Western Ghats and the landscape changes dramatically: you pass from the dry Tamil Nadu plains to Kerala's green hills covered with tea, coffee, and spice plantations. The final winding stretch through the mountains is spectacular. Arrive in late afternoon in Kumily, the gateway village to the Periyar Reserve.

Visit a spice garden in the Kumily area to understand how black pepper, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, and vanilla grow. The guides will have you smell, taste, and touch the plants—you'll never look at your spice rack the same way again. Kerala cardamom is considered the finest in the world. Allow 1 to 1.5 hours for the visit.

activities.text: In the evening, don't miss a Kathakali performance, Kerala's traditional dance-theater. The dancers, made up over 2 hours before the performance, interpret episodes from the Mahabharata and Ramayana with codified facial expressions and spectacular costumes. Operators offer performances in Kumily—arrive 30 minutes before the start to watch the makeup application, which is almost as fascinating as the show itself.

days_plan.itin_title: Tamil Nadu and Kerala Road Trip: Temples and Backwaters

visits.text: Start with Padmanabhaswamy Temple in the heart of Trivandrum's East Fort. This temple dedicated to Vishnu blends Kerala and Dravidian architectural styles—its seven-tier gopuram is covered in finely chiseled sculptures. Inside, the deity's idol measures 5.5 meters long and reclines on the serpent Anantha, visible through three separate doors. In 2011, the opening of its vaults revealed a treasure estimated at $22 billion, making it the world's richest temple. Important note: only Hindus may enter, and there's a strict dress code—men must wear a dhoti (available for rent at the entrance) and remove their upper garment.

Just beside the temple, step into Kuthiramalika Palace. Built in the 1840s by Maharaja Swathi Thirunal, a musician and patron of the arts, this palace of teak and rosewood takes its name from the 122 horses carved into the brackets that support the southern roof. Of its 80 rooms, only 20 are open to the public—you'll see two royal thrones, one fashioned from 24 elephant tusks, the other from Bohemian crystal. Don't miss the musical tree, an object that produces eight different sounds when struck in different places. Closed Mondays.

Late in the day, head to Kovalam, 16 km south of Trivandrum. This former fishing village became famous in the 1930s when the Queen Regent of Travancore had Halcyon Castle built here. Three crescent beaches follow one another: Lighthouse Beach is the liveliest, Hawa Beach draws Indian families, and Samudra Beach remains the quietest. Settle in at Lighthouse Beach for sunset—the golden light on the coconut palms and fishing nets is a sight not to be missed. If you have time, climb the Vizhinjam lighthouse for a panoramic view of the coast.

activities.text: In the evening, sit down for a Kerala seafood dinner facing the Arabian Sea. The beachfront restaurants in Kovalam serve grilled fish, king prawns, and crab masala accompanied by rice and coconut curry. If you're curious, try the karimeen pollichathu, a local fish cooked in a banana leaf—it's one of Kerala's signature dishes.

To recover from jet lag, book an Ayurvedic massage at one of Kovalam's wellness centers. Kerala is the birthplace of Ayurveda, and Kovalam has a large number of traditional centers. Expect about an hour for an abhyanga, the classic warm oil massage.

days_plan.itin_title: South India Circuit: Temples, Backwaters & Wellness

visits.text: The Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple in Srirangam, a district of Trichy, is the largest functioning Hindu temple in the world: 63 hectares, 7 concentric enclosures, 21 gopurams and 50 shrines. Built from the 10th century onwards by the Chola, it was expanded by the Pandya, Hoysala and Nayak over the centuries. The Rajagopuram (royal tower), completed in 1987, rises to 73 meters.

From the visitor-accessible areas on the roofs of the temple's outer galleries, you'll have a striking view of the entire complex—the colorful gopurams stretch on endlessly. A fascinating detail: the Orlov Diamond, now displayed in the Moscow Kremlin, is said to have been stolen from the idol in this temple by a French deserter in the 18th century.

Round out the day with Trichy's Rock Fort Temple, perched on an 83-meter rocky outcrop in the city center. The 437 steps carved into the rock lead to the summit, where the view takes in Srirangam, the Cauvery River, and the surrounding plain. The rock itself is 3.8 billion years old—one of the oldest rock outcrops on Earth.

activities.text: Srirangam's ritual atmosphere peaks during evening prayer: oil lamps illuminate the corridors of sculpted columns and priests' chanting reverberates through the galleries. If you're here in December–January, the Vaikunta Ekadasi festival draws a million pilgrims over 21 days—spectacular but crowded.

days_plan.itin_title: Tamil Nadu and Kerala Road Trip: Temples and Backwaters

visits.text: You don't need to be Hindu to be struck by Tirumala: the Venkateswara temple, on the Seven Peaks hills at an elevation of 853 meters, receives tens of thousands of pilgrims every day, according to Britannica. Dedicated to Venkateswara, an avatar of Vishnu, it's reputed to be the world's richest and most visited Hindu temple. The complex covers 16.2 acres. Book your darshan ahead through the TTD website or buy the paid “Sudarshana” ticket to avoid queues lasting several hours.

activities.text: You take the free pilgrims' bus from lower Tirupati up to Tirumala: nineteen kilometers of winding ascent through the Seshachalam hills, with brief glimpses of the forest. An alternative to traveling to darshan by private car, and often faster at peak hours. Last departure generally around 10 p.m.

visits.text: Transit day: Jaisalmer → Udaipur is the trickiest leg of the trip. There's no direct train between the two cities. The best option is an overnight bus (roughly 10–11 hours, departing around 5–6 PM, arriving early morning) or going via Jodhpur by train (5 hours) then Jodhpur → Udaipur by car or bus (5 hours). Either way, you'll arrive in the morning. Rest at your hotel before hitting the sights in the early afternoon.

Head to the City Palace of Udaipur — the largest palace in Rajasthan, a complex stretching 244 metres long and 30 metres high, built over four centuries starting in 1559 by Udai Singh II, the city's founder. It towers over Lake Pichola from a rocky ridge. Inside, lose yourself in the maze of courtyards, balconies and chambers adorned with mirror mosaics and painted frescoes. The museum displays Rajput miniatures, weapons and royal cradles — allow at least 1.5 hours.

The Jagdish Temple, steps away from the City Palace, is a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu, built in 1651. Its 24-metre façade is covered in sculptures of dancers, elephants and horsemen. You'll recognise it by the statue of Garuda (Vishnu's eagle mount) guarding the entrance.

The Monsoon Palace (Sajjangarh) sits atop the Aravalli hills, 5 km from the centre — built in 1884 by Maharana Sajjan Singh to observe the monsoon clouds, it was never completed. The winding road up passes through forested land. From the summit, you look down over all of Udaipur, its lakes and hills stretching as far as the eye can see. Take an auto-rickshaw up in the morning for the best light.

Saheliyon Ki Bari (the Garden of the Maids of Honour) is a small ornamental garden built in the 18th century by Maharana Sangram Singh II for the 48 handmaidens who came as part of his queen's dowry. Fountains, lotus ponds and shaded pavilions — a peaceful place away from the bustle of the markets.
Take a walk around Fateh Sagar Lake, Udaipur's second lake — a pleasant stroll along the banks. Boats shuttle visitors to Nehru Park, a small garden island in the middle of the lake.

activities.text: In the late afternoon, take a boat ride on Lake Pichola — the hour-long trip circles Jag Mandir and Jag Niwas (the Lake Palace, now a luxury hotel that appears to float on the water). The lake was created in 1362 and expanded by successive maharanas. The golden evening light on the white palaces is Udaipur's crowning moment.

In the evening, step inside Bagore Ki Haveli, an 18th-century haveli turned museum. A traditional Rajasthani dance performance takes place every evening at 7 PM in the courtyard — Ghoomar dances, puppet shows and acrobats. It's touristy but well done, and the candlelit courtyard has a warm atmosphere.

Visit Shilpgram, a reconstructed craft village 3 km from Fateh Sagar — 26 traditional huts representing the architectural styles of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Goa and Maharashtra. Artisans work in front of visitors: pottery, weaving, wood carving. It's a good place to buy genuine handicrafts at fair prices.

In the evening, organise your departure to Mumbai. The Mewar Express (train 12964) leaves Udaipur City at 6:15 PM bound for Hazrat Nizamuddin (Delhi) — but for Mumbai, take an overnight bus or a domestic flight (1 hour 15 minutes) instead. Another option: a train from Udaipur → Ahmedabad (6–7 hours) then Ahmedabad → Mumbai (6–7 hours), but that's a long journey. The flight is recommended if your budget allows.

visits.text: Four times the area of Buckingham Palace. Yet Vadodara's Laxmi Vilas Palace has remained the private residence of the Gaekwads of Baroda since its construction in 1890 by Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III. Architect Major Charles Mant created an Indo-Saracenic synthesis: Mughal domes, Gothic arches, mashrabiya windows. A section is open to the public with an audio guide. Closed Monday.

The Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum, in the palace outbuildings, presents European paintings and sculptures assembled by the Gaekwads in the 19th century. The collection surprises with its eclecticism: Raphael sits alongside Tanjore, and neoclassical bronzes stand beside Mughal miniatures. Ten minutes' walk from the main palace.

activities.text: Stroll through Sayaji Baug: a 113-acre royal garden crossed by the Vishwamitri River, housing a museum, a zoo, and Baroda Gallery—one of India's oldest public art collections. Ideal in the late afternoon when the heat subsides and families fill the paths.

days_plan.itin_title: Gujarat: Grand Tour of UNESCO Sites in 15 Days

visits.text: Domestic flight Khajuraho → Varanasi (around 1 hour 30 minutes with a connection or direct if available). You arrive in Varanasi—also called Benares or Kashi. Nothing prepares you for the sensory shock of the ghats beside the Ganges: the funeral pyres of Manikarnika burning 24 hours a day, ash-covered sadhus, female buffaloes bathing, fishing boats and children playing cricket—all at once, within 50 meters. Start by walking down the steps of Dashashwamedh Ghat, the main ghat, and let the scene draw you in.

Lose yourself in the old city's lanes (galis) - a labyrinth so narrow even rickshaws can't pass. Shops overflow with Benares silk saris, jewelry, colored powders, and sweets. You'll encounter tiny temples at every corner, sacred cows, funeral processions, and playing children. It's India's most organized chaos.

Visit Kashi Vishwanath Temple (Golden Temple), one of the 12 most sacred Shiva jyotirlingas. The current temple dates from 1780, built by Queen Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore, after the previous one was destroyed by Aurangzeb. The dome is covered with 820 kg of gold donated by Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Access for non-Hindus may be restricted to certain areas—inquire beforehand.

Wake before dawn for a sunrise boat ride on the Ganges—this is THE magical moment in Varanasi. Mist rises over the river, the first golden rays touch the ghats, devotees descend the steps for ritual ablutions, and pyres smoke gently. Your boatman will take you along the 84 ghats over about 5 km—each has its specialty and history. Manikarnika is the main cremation ghat, where pyres never go out. Stay respectful and don't photograph cremations.

After breakfast, take an auto-rickshaw to Sarnath (10 km, 30 min), the place where Buddha gave his first sermon after enlightenment—an event known as “Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma.” The Dhamek Stupa, a massive 43-meter-high cylinder adorned with Gupta-era floral motifs, marks the exact spot. The Ashoka pillar that stood here bore the famous four-lion capital that became India's national emblem (visible on every rupee note).

Sarnath's archaeological museum preserves the original of Ashoka's four-lion capital (4th century BC), along with Buddhist sculptures of extraordinary grace - notably a Gupta-era Buddha considered one of the world's finest. Allow at least 45 minutes.

Back in Varanasi, walk down to Assi Ghat, the southernmost ghat, calmer than Dashashwamedh. It's the meeting point for Benares intellectuals and artists - you'll find small cafés and a relaxed vibe. The morning aarti (Subah-e-Banaras) here is more intimate than Dashashwamedh's evening one.

activities.text: In the evening, attend Ganga Aarti at Dashashwamedh Ghat. Seven young priests in saffron robes perform synchronized movements with multi-tiered oil lamps, while mantras and bells echo in the incense-laden air. The ceremony lasts 45 minutes and begins at sunset (6pm in winter, 7pm in summer). Arrive 1 hour early for a good spot on the steps, or book a boat on the Ganges to watch the spectacle from the water - it's even more impressive.
Taste silver-leaf lassi in old city shops, morning kachori sabzi, and chena dahi vada (lentil fritters with yogurt). Varanasi street food is legendary - and entirely vegetarian in the old city.

Visit a Benares silk weaving workshop (Banarasi saree). The silk saris woven here, with gold and silver motifs, are among India's most precious textiles. Some workshops welcome visitors and will show you the painstaking work on the loom—a sari can take from 15 days to 6 months of work.

Late in the day, detour to the campus of Banaras Hindu University (BHU), one of Asia's largest universities, founded in 1916. Bharat Kala Bhavan, its museum, houses a remarkable collection of Indian miniatures, sculptures, and old textiles.

visits.text: The drive from Kollam to Varkala is short (40 km, 1 hour)—you'll arrive mid-morning. Varkala is the antithesis of Kerala's flat beaches: here, reddish laterite cliffs 15 to 20 meters high plunge straight into the Arabian Sea. The path along the clifftop, lined with cafés, boutiques, and bougainvillea, is one of South India's loveliest coastal walks.

Descend the steps to Papanasam Beach, the main beach at the cliff's foot. Its name means "destruction of sins" in Sanskrit—Hindus believe bathing here washes away sins. The beach is monitored by lifeguards, but watch for currents—they can be strong, especially during the monsoon. Early morning, you'll see fishermen hauling nets onto the sand.

Dedicate the morning to a surf lesson on Papanasam or Black Beach. Local operators offer beginner sessions of 1.5 to 2 hours, equipment included. Waves are moderate and suited to beginners—it's one of Kerala's best learning spots. Book early morning when waves and heat are gentler.

Visit Janardhana Swami Temple, a shrine dedicated to Vishnu over 2,000 years old, perched on the cliff above Papanasam Beach. The temple is an important pilgrimage site—Keralans perform funerary rites by the sea here. The interior is reserved for Hindus, but the exterior architecture, sculptures, and atmosphere are worth the visit. A great sacred banyan shades the entrance.

In the afternoon, push north to Kappil Beach, 6 km from Varkala. This beach is bordered by a lagoon—the mouth of the Edava River meets the sea in a landscape of sand, freshwater, and coconut palms. Much quieter than Papanasam, it's ideal for a calm swim or a picnic.

activities.text: Settle on the clifftop for sunset—it's Varkala's daily ritual. Terrace cafés fill up as the sun descends toward the horizon. The vibe is laid-back, almost hippie—far from the mass tourism of Goa. If you fancy an Ayurvedic massage, reputable centers along the cliff offer traditional treatments. Stick with those affiliated with the Kerala government for quality.

Late in the day, join a Keralan cooking class. Operators in Varkala offer 2- to 3-hour workshops where you'll learn to prepare a tamarind fish curry, appam (fermented rice pancake), and payasam (coconut milk dessert). You cook and eat your own meal—a delicious way to close your penultimate evening in Kerala.

visits.text: The golden grass ripples, and suddenly a hundred antelopes emerge in formation—Velavadar Blackbuck National Park is home to one of India's largest populations of spiral-horned antelopes (blackbucks). The flat savanna allows sightings at long distances without dense vegetation. The park also shelters Indian wolves and numerous migratory raptors in winter.

activities.text: Velavadar Blackbuck National Park, established in 1976 over 34 km², was once the hunting ground of the Maharaja of Bhavnagar. Today, safaris by jeep or on foot allow visitors to approach the herds at close range. It's also one of the world's best sites for observing hovering harriers in winter—a phenomenon ornithologists come specifically to document.

days_plan.itin_title: Gujarat: Grand Tour of UNESCO Sites in 15 Days

visits.text: Modest in appearance, the Undavalli Caves hide a treasure of Indian rock-cut architecture ten kilometers from Vijayawada. These sandstone caves, carved between the 4th and 7th centuries, house on the second floor a monumental statue of reclining Vishnu sculpted from a single granite block. The ensemble reflects the successive influence of Jain, Buddhist, and Hindu worship. Open 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.; bring sturdy shoes for the stairs.

Andhras simply call her “Kanaka Durgamma”—the golden goddess of Vijayawada. The Kanaka Durga temple stands atop Indrakeeladri hill, on the banks of the Krishna. Its current structure dates back at least to the 10th century. The eight-armed goddess, standing atop the demon Mahishasura, is adorned each day with different ornaments according to the ritual calendar. Queues can be long on weekends.

Industrial and densely built, Vijayawada hides this barrage that doubles as a promenade on the Krishna: the Prakasam Barrage, built in 1957 and stretching several kilometers, links the Krishna and Guntur districts. In the evening, lights illuminate the flowing water. Unobstructed view of the river, with the temple hill in the background.

In 1360, the Reddi kings built Kondapalli Fort on a hill overlooking the plain: the main entrance gate, carved from a single granite block, still stands. Having passed to the Qutubshahis in the 16th century, then to the British, this eighteen-square-kilometer fort twenty-four kilometers from Vijayawada attracts few visitors despite what it has to offer. The Tanisha Mahal, a palace perched on a ridge between two peaks, is worth the climb. The neighboring village is also known for its colorful wooden toys.

activities.text: You cross the Prakasam Barrage on foot at sunset, between the two banks of the Krishna. Wind comes off the river, fishermen cast their lines from the parapet, a few families have spread mats. The city seems distant during these twenty minutes of walking.

If you have time, head to the village of Kondapalli, about half an hour's drive from Vijayawada: artisans carve their toys from soft Tella Poniki wood in houses opening onto the street. The style - lively, colorful mythological figures - goes back several generations. You can buy directly from the families, without a middleman.

India's East Coast: Chennai to Visakhapatnam, 13 Days

visits.text: Built in 1969 by the Soviets, INS Kursura is a 91.3-meter S20 patrol boat that has been beached on Ramakrishna Beach since 2002—India's first submarine museum. You visit the crew quarters, torpedo room, and command post through corridors so narrow that you get a tangible sense of what it means to live beneath the sea. She served in the 1971 Indo-Pakistani War. Closed Mondays.

From the summit of Kailasagiri, a 360° view of the sea and city opens up from a height of 110 meters. This 380-acre park houses two giant statues of Shiva and Parvati in brilliant white, visible from the coastal highway. Access is on foot or by cable car. Best sunset in Vizag, according to regulars.

RK Beach is Vizag's liveliest city beach—and at the same time one of the most accessible. The Victory at Sea Memorial, Visakha Museum, and promenade run directly along the waterfront. Avoid weekend peak hours if you're seeking tranquility.

Rushikonda is Vizag's best beach—this is where regulars come on weekdays to avoid the crowds. Golden sand, wooded hills in the background, and waters of the Bay of Bengal where you can swim under supervision. Blue Flag certified (with ups and downs depending on the audits), it's one of Andhra Pradesh's best-maintained beaches. Water sports available all day.

Fishermen still come here before dawn, as Yarada Beach has kept its fishing-village character 15 km from central Vizag. The beach is tucked between the hills of Dolphin's Nose and the sea. The currents are strong - no swimming. Sensitive military area: drones are strictly prohibited.

activities.text: You take the cable car to the top of Kailasagiri: the gondola rises slowly above the coconut palms and Vizag's coastline unfolds in an arc. The walk down along the park trail takes an extra hour and is worth the detour.

If you enjoy water sports, Rushikonda offers water skiing, windsurfing, and jet ski outings directly on the beach. Operators are present from 9 a.m. Rates vary by season; negotiate in the morning before the afternoon rush.

visits.text: A provincial town with little apparent glamour, yet Vizianagaram Fort holds a century of Pusapati royalty. Built in 1713 by Vijaya Rama Raju, it houses temples and palaces. The main entrance, Nagar Khana (“drum house”), has elaborate architecture. Now partly occupied by a college, the fort is freely accessible.

activities.text: Founded in 1713 by Vijaya Rama Raju, Vizianagaram Fort was established on Vijaya Dashami—a day said to bear the five “signs of victory.” Allow 45 minutes for the full visit.

days_plan.itin_title: From Coast to Jungle: Bhubaneswar to Bhopal in 16 Days

visits.text: Warangal Fort lies in ruins, but its four Kakatiya arches—the Kirti Toranas—stand amid the void, carved with divine figures and floral motifs, among the Deccan's finest. The circular enclosure dates from the 12th century. Go early: shade vanishes quickly under this sun.

A thousand black basalt pillars support Hanamkonda's Thousand Pillar Temple, erected in 1163 by King Rudra Deva. Star-shaped plan on a six-foot platform, triple sanctuary dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu, and Surya: this is a Trikutalayam. The interior temperature remains surprisingly cool even in summer.

Climb to Bhadrakali Temple, perched between Warangal and Hanamkonda, to see Bhadrakali Lake and the natural rock formations encircling the sanctuary. Panoramic view over the plain. Arrive late afternoon: the raking light transforms the stone.

activities.text: Warangal's market merits an hour for its local textiles and Deccan spices. The area around the railway station concentrates fabric shops; prices are fixed in cooperatives and negotiable with independent merchants.

visits.text: If you arrive early, Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple at Yadagirigutta reveals its five forms of Narasimha in a natural cave beneath the rock, before the queue swells. The sanctuary was entirely rebuilt in black granite and inaugurated in March 2022. Plan for shoe deposit and modest dress.
